text:
**Ohio's Senate and governor races have tightened into genuine toss-ups, with Democrats holding narrow edges in most recent polling just two weeks before Election Day.**[[1]](https://t.co/ROn3Ee8a9u)

[Take 10/15 · D-5]
**What people think this is about:** After years of Republican dominance in Ohio presidential voting and state offices, the 2026 midterms have suddenly made the state competitive again, with national stakes for Senate control and the first Democratic governor in 15 years.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** Both parties are pouring resources into turnout and persuasion in a state where early voting data shows Democrats banking a substantial lead among those who have already cast ballots, while Republicans rely on stronger Election Day performance and national messaging to close gaps that have narrowed since 2024.[[2]](https://t.co/QbCkeqPkH9)

**Observations**
- Polling averages place the Senate race (Brown vs. Husted) at roughly Brown +2.8 to +3.1 among likely voters, a toss-up rating from forecasters, with Marist showing Brown +4 and ActiVote a virtual tie as of mid-to-late October.[[3]](https://t.co/fAvI4IvZtr)
- The governor race (Acton vs. Ramaswamy) shows similar tightness, with Acton ahead by about 4-5 points in most nonpartisan averages but some Republican-leaning polls flipping the lead; Cook Political Report rates it a toss-up.[[4]](https://t.co/zmJscDlVCH)
- Early voting (about 20% of likely voters in one October survey) breaks heavily Democratic—nearly 40 points in one poll—while Republicans hold an edge among those planning to vote on Election Day, highlighting turnout as the decisive variable.[[2]](https://t.co/QbCkeqPkH9)
- Ohio's shift from reliable Republican presidential territory (Trump won by double digits in 2024) to battleground status stems from voter dissatisfaction with economic conditions and split-ticket tendencies, not a wholesale realignment.
- National implications are real: a Democratic Senate flip or first Dem governor since 2011 would amplify midterm narratives of backlash, while Republican holds would reinforce the state's rightward drift outside these specific contests.
- Both races feature high spending and national surrogates, with Democrats emphasizing local economic grievances and Republicans leaning on Trump-era branding and base mobilization.

**Snapshot**  
As of October 19-20, 2026, Ohio has emerged as a key midterm battleground after years of GOP dominance in presidential and many state races. The U.S. Senate special/general contest pits Democrat Sherrod Brown against Republican Jon Husted in a race rated a toss-up, while the open governor's race features Democrat Amy Acton versus Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, also viewed as highly competitive. Recent Marist and other polls show narrow Democratic edges among likely voters, though results vary by pollster and early voting patterns favor Democrats.[[5]](https://t.co/2Ara2qrqX7)

**Timeline of material facts**  
- **2024 presidential**: Trump wins Ohio by double digits, continuing the state's Republican lean in national elections.  
- **2025-early 2026 primaries**: Ramaswamy secures GOP nomination for governor; Brown and Husted emerge as Senate contenders.  
- **September-October 2026**: Multiple polls (Marist, BGSU/YouGov, CNN/SSRS, NYT/Siena, ActiVote) show both races within single digits, with averages tightening into toss-up territory.[[6]](https://t.co/GTJRdpiGXZ)  
- **Mid-October 2026**: Early voting data indicates strong Democratic performance among those who have voted; Marist (Oct 15-18) releases Brown +4 and Acton +7 among likely voters.[[1]](https://t.co/ROn3Ee8a9u)  
- **October 18-19, 2026**: ActiVote polls show near-ties or slight Republican edges in head-to-heads; forecasters maintain toss-up ratings.  
- **October 19-20, 2026**: Media highlights Ohio as battleground with national stakes for Senate control and state executive power.[[5]](https://t.co/2Ara2qrqX7)

**Sides**  
**Democrats (Brown/Acton campaigns and allies) (IT/LT mix)**: Steelman — Brown brings decades of Senate experience fighting for manufacturing and trade protections in a Rust Belt state; Acton positions as a fresh, competent alternative focused on state issues like healthcare and education. Independents and suburban voters are breaking their way in recent surveys, reflecting economic discontent.  
**Critique**: LT — Polls confirm narrow leads in several surveys. IT — Early vote advantage is real but Election Day voters lean the other direction; over-reliance on turnout models risks disappointment if GOP mobilization succeeds.  

**Republicans (Husted/Ramaswamy campaigns and Trump-aligned forces) (IT/LT mix)**: Steelman — Husted as incumbent brings name recognition and alignment with Trump/Vance priorities; Ramaswamy offers high-energy outsider appeal and self-funding. The state's presidential results and rural/suburban base provide a structural floor.  
**Critique**: LT — Some polls (ActiVote, Rasmussen) show them competitive or ahead. IT — National brand and base enthusiasm have not yet translated into consistent polling leads; early voting deficit creates a steeper climb.  

**Technocrat vs. Populist Realist patterns**: Technocrats emphasize polling models and generic ballot trends; populist realists stress on-the-ground turnout realities and voter anger over economic conditions.

**Rumsfeld Matrix**  
- **Known Knowns**: Both races are toss-ups per Cook and polling averages; early voting favors Democrats; Ohio shifted right in presidential voting but these down-ballot contests remain fluid.  
- **Known Unknowns**: Exact Election Day turnout split and late shifts among independents; precise impact of national economic messaging.  
- **Unknown Knowns**: Detailed county-level early vote breakdowns and internal campaign data on persuasion vs. mobilization effectiveness.  
- **Unknown Unknowns**: Black-swan events (scandals, economic surprises, or weather on Nov 3) that could swing low-propensity voters.

**Incentives map**  
Democrats benefit from framing these as referenda on the national environment and economic dissatisfaction to maximize early and suburban turnout. Republicans gain from tying candidates to Trump-era strength and base enthusiasm to offset early vote gaps. Media and pollsters gain engagement from "battleground" narratives. Both parties treat Ohio as a test of whether 2024 realignment holds or midterms revert to historical patterns. Attention economy rewards tight polls over structural context.

**Dueling AI advice**  
**Moral AI Advice**: Focus on verifiable turnout data and economic indicators rather than narrative momentum. The side that best matches voter pocketbook reality on Election Day wins; models are tools, not destiny.  

**Evil AI Advice**: Flood the zone with ads exploiting whichever side's early vote lead looks scariest, then claim vindication no matter the result—engagement pays either way.

**Practical takeaway**  
- Watch final early vote totals and Election Day modeling for the real margin.  
- Discount single polls; averages and trends matter more.  
- Track independent and suburban shifts in the last 10 days.  
- Note that a Democratic win here would signal broader midterm headwinds; a Republican hold would confirm structural advantages.  
- Primary sources (Marist, BGSU/YouGov, ActiVote releases) beat secondary spin.

**What would falsify this read**  
- A final pre-election average showing either race outside 5 points with consistent methodology.  
- Early vote data reversing to show Republican dominance.  
- Post-election analysis proving one candidate overperformed or underperformed fundamentals by double digits due to unique factors.  
- National generic ballot shifting dramatically in the final week.

text:
AI News — Oct 21, 2026

The PyTorch war is on. Google open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for its TPUs, one day after Amazon shipped TorchNeuron for Trainium. Existing PyTorch apps can move over largely through configuration, with torch.compile support and an agent suite to help with migration. Why it matters: CUDA-first PyTorch has been Nvidia's quiet moat. Two hyperscalers now offer a no-rewrite exit, which is real pricing leverage for anyone with a big training or inference bill.

Washington vs DeepSeek. The US barred federal civilian agencies from using DeepSeek products, and China condemned the move. The same day, DeepSeek open-sourced the inference software it runs its own models on, aimed at cutting serving costs. The policy wall goes up while the open-source pressure on OpenAI and Anthropic's serving economics keeps rising.

AI doing science, failures included. Anthropic says Claude autonomously designed protein binders against five scorpion neurotoxins: 318,484 designs in 64 hours. Of 211 lab-tested candidates (with Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience), 17 met binding criteria. Anthropic makes no antivenom claim and is releasing all 211 designs plus the data. The honest hit rate is the story.

OpenAI pushes deeper into pharma. It's acquiring Orchestra Bio and folding its drug-development coordination platform into its Rosalind life-sciences suite. It also published 722 math manuscripts from an internal frontier model, with Lean proof formalizations.

Meta's compute flex. Meta detailed Prometheus in Ohio: phase one is complete and trained its Muse models, it's scaling toward ~1M GPUs, and pretraining goodput tops 85%.

My take (opinion): the moat is shifting from chips to software portability, and from benchmarks to verifiable real-world output. Watch how Nvidia responds on developer lock-in.

text:
I’m more interested in how many shares each side gets than in putting Tesla and SpaceX under one roof.

Both companies have formed independent board committees to discuss a possible merger. There’s still no announced deal. Until there are terms, liking the idea doesn’t tell shareholders much about whether they’d be getting a fair price.

Tesla holders would be buying into Starlink, the launch business, and SpaceX’s AI operations. Starlink brings subscription revenue, but the satellites need replacing, rockets need developing, and the AI business needs expensive computing capacity. Those spending decisions would become part of the investment they already own.

That could be attractive at the right price. It could also leave Tesla shareholders giving up too much of their company for businesses they could buy separately.

SpaceX holders would have the same concern in reverse. They’d gain Tesla’s automotive and energy businesses, along with exposure to vehicle discounts, factory spending, and whatever happens to demand for its next models. Someone who bought SpaceX for satellite broadband may not want their returns tied to the next quarter’s car deliveries.

And SpaceX is already public. It doesn’t need a Tesla merger to give investors a stock they can trade. Shareholders can already own both companies and choose the balance themselves.

So a deal needs to offer something worth giving up that choice for. Sharing technology or coordinating projects might help, but the committees would still need to explain why those benefits require a merger and how much shareholders should pay for them.

The exchange ratio is where that gets uncomfortable. A higher valuation for SpaceX means its holders receive more of the combined company, leaving Tesla holders with less. A higher valuation for Tesla does the reverse. Calling both businesses part of the same long-term vision doesn’t settle that negotiation.

I can see why someone would want to own both. I’d still want to see the proposed share split before supporting a merger.

text:
America can launch the rocket. Can it build the next thousand?

Rockets lifting off. Cars testing aerospace thrusters. American engineering knows how to command attention.

But behind the spectacle is a story that matters to workers, taxpayers and anyone concerned about national security: America’s capacity to turn ambitious designs into sustained production.

The latest Federal Reserve figures offer an encouraging signal. Defense and space equipment output rose 6.7% over the year ending in September, compared with 1.1% for manufacturing overall.

That is a strong pocket of growth within an uneven manufacturing economy—and a reason to look beyond the launch footage.

SpaceX’s reusable rockets put engineering, manufacturing and operational experience on display. Tesla’s Roadster ambitions raise another question: How does an attention-grabbing demonstration become a repeatable product?

And Anduril founder Palmer Luckey brings the discussion straight to America’s factory floor:

“We need to design missiles that can be made in car factories.”

Think about what that means.

The workers building cars, tractors and industrial equipment hold skills that could help determine how quickly America can respond to a national emergency. Their factories, tools and suppliers belong in the conversation about military preparedness.

Luckey’s challenge is to design weapons with the country’s existing manufacturing capabilities in mind.

Because an arsenal begins long before a weapon reaches the battlefield. It begins with engineers, machinists, production lines, components and suppliers that can deliver.

A successful launch demonstrates capability. A prototype demonstrates possibility. Sustained production tests whether American industry can deliver reliably and at scale.

That is where these stories meet—and where citizens should keep watching.

What is actually reaching production?
Can suppliers keep up?
Are we building the workforce and industrial capacity the country needs?
The spectacle earns the headlines. The ability to build what comes next deserves our attention.

text:
Robert Hickman split rails in Missouri while Lincoln got famous for it.

He was enslaved in Boone County, doing the work that put Abraham Lincoln on campaign posters. When the Emancipation Proclamation took effect on January 1, 1863, it did not reach him. Missouri was a border state and the border states were left out of it. So in May he took his wife, his children and about seventy-five other people onto the water and went north without waiting for anyone's permission.

The boat that found them was not going where they thought it was going.

The Northerner came up to the Lowertown levee at St. Paul on May 6, 1863. A crowd was already on the landing, most of it Irish laborers, and it would not let anybody off.

David Vassar Taylor's account gives the reason without decoration. The men on the levee were afraid the new arrivals would take their work.

They had some basis for the arithmetic. There were 259 Black people in the whole state of Minnesota in 1860, and by 1870 there would be 759. Nearly all of that increase came up the river on boats like this one.

The Saint Paul Press watched the morning from the dock and printed what it saw. An honest onlooker, the paper wrote, would have ranked the people on the boat a good deal higher than the crowd screaming at them.

The captain did not argue with the levee.

He took the Northerner back out into the channel and ran it a few miles upriver to Fort Snelling. That is where everyone aboard first stood on ground where nobody could be owned.

The boat had a reason to be on that stretch of water. It was carrying contraband teamsters and laborers up from St. Louis at the request of Henry H. Sibley, who had finished a term as governor of Minnesota and was then a colonel of the state militia.

The state was short of men. Soldiers had gone to the Civil War and to the U.S.-Dakota War, and the fields were standing unworked. In 1863 the Saint Paul Press reported that five thousand workers were wanted.

The same paper explained why the wanted workers were Black ones. Hired Black labor, it said, was "more tractable and more docile" than the white labor usually available for the job.

That was the offer, printed in the newspaper of the state capital.

The Northerner had a second errand in Minnesota, and it is the part of this day that rarely gets told.

William D. Green's account has the boat coming north under government order to carry Dakota people out of the state. Fort Snelling, where it had just put its passengers ashore, was where Dakota women, children and elders had been held through the winter of 1862 and 1863.

Green describes the two groups passing each other at the landing. One walked off the boat onto free ground. The other walked past the site of its own confinement and up the same gangway.

Hickman's people watched that on their first afternoon in the north.

They stayed at the fort through the summer and the fall. Ten days behind them, on May 15, 1863, a steamboat called the Davenport landed two hundred and eighteen more Black arrivals under military escort, and the welcome at the water's edge was the same one.

Then the city authorities split the new arrivals up. Some were sent to Duluth, some to Hastings, some to farms further south, and the rest were allowed to stay in St. Paul.

Hickman stayed, and so did most of the people who had come up with him.

His owner in Missouri had taught him to read and had let him preach to the others on the surrounding places, which is how a man with no standing anywhere came to be leading seventy-six people onto a river.

His wife Minta had been born around 1837 and was held by a different owner, a man who lived near his own. Both of those owners died before the war started, and it changed nothing about who belonged to whom.

The family had gone first to a contraband camp at St. Louis in the spring of 1863. The people who came up out of it with them were calling themselves Pilgrims by the time they reached St. Paul.

Their first gathering in the city was in a house on Fifth Street between Washington and Franklin, belonging to a woman named Caroline Nelson. She had been in St. Paul since about 1850, had started out taking in washing, and by then was working as a midwife.

By November 1863 they had rented a room of their own. It was the Good Templars' lodge room in the Concert Hall Building on Third Street, taken from a temperance society that had it first.

Two months of planning followed, and then they hit the rule.

A congregation could not incorporate without an ordained minister. Hickman was not one, and in Minnesota in 1864 there was no route open to him to become one.

So in January 1864 they took mission status under the First Baptist Church of St. Paul and kept meeting on their own under Hickman. That arrangement held for the next two years.

Then they went to First Baptist's trustees with a request. There was a lot on Sibley Street near Morris Street worth two hundred dollars, and they asked that congregation's trustees to buy it and hold it in trust for them.

The ground was bought, and the name on it was not theirs.

Pilgrim Baptist was formally organized on November 15, 1866, the first Black congregation in the state. They marked it with a baptismal service on the bank of the Mississippi, the river that had carried most of them there.

The charter roll still carries the names. Fielding and Adeline Combs, Henry and Charlotte Moffit, John B. and Elizabeth Trotter, Giles Crenshaw, and the Hickmans.

Hickman was not the minister of it.

From 1866 to 1877 the pulpit at Pilgrim Baptist was held by two white ministers out of First Baptist, William Norris and Andrew Torbert. The congregation had been assembled by a man who could not stand in front of it in any official capacity, so other men were sent to do that.

He spent those eleven years working through the requirements for ordination.

The church was incorporated in 1870. First Baptist of St. Anthony handed over part of a building it was about to tear down, and that timber went into the first structure the congregation ever put up for itself, finished at Twelfth and Cedar.

He was still not its minister when it opened the doors.

On the evening of November 18, 1868, a meeting was called in the room Pilgrim Baptist used as a church. It had nothing to do with the church.

Two weeks earlier Minnesota had voted to erase the word white from the section of its constitution that set out who could vote. The official canvass came back 39,493 for and 30,121 against, which put the state two years ahead of the rest of the country.

In St. Paul, the city with the largest Black population in Minnesota, the majority voted the other way.

Until that count, Black men in the state could not vote, could not hold office and could not sit on a jury.

The men who gathered in the church room that night resolved to call a statewide convention of Black Minnesotans, and appointed eighteen of themselves to arrange it. The printed proceedings record remarks that evening from Jernigan, Edwards, Jackson and Hickman.

What any of them actually said is not in the record. The committee list is, and Robert Hickman's name is printed second on it, directly under Maurice Jernigan's.

Three of those eighteen names are Combs, Moffit and Trotter. Those same three surnames sit on Pilgrim Baptist's charter roll.

The convention met at Ingersoll Hall in St. Paul on January 1, 1869, and the men who called it decorated the stage themselves. They hung flags and portraits of Lincoln, Grant, Frederick Douglass and Henry Highland Garnet. Beside all of it they hung one of the spears John Brown's party had carried at Harpers Ferry.

The governor came and spoke. So did the mayor of St. Paul, in a city that had voted no.

Two months later Robert Hickman was among the first Black men seated on a jury in Minnesota. The Minneapolis Daily Tribune covered it on March 25, 1869.

Three weeks before he sat, on March 4, 1869, a law had taken effect pulling state funding from any Minnesota district that kept Black children out of its schools.

The ordination came, and the record cannot agree on when.

The African American Registry has him licensed in 1874 and ordained the year after. David Vassar Taylor puts the ordination at 1877. The National Park Service says 1874, and says plainly that the reason it took that long was that he was a Black man.

The accounts converge on 1878, the year Pilgrim Baptist became his to lead, and on 1886, the year he retired from it. He was forty-seven at the first and fifty-five at the second.

In between he used the church to start two more, Zion Baptist in Minneapolis and a mission at Hastings.

Robert Hickman died in St. Paul in 1900. The National Park Service page on him gives February 6 in its text and February 16 in the box at the top, and lists Oakland Cemetery.

The record still argues about the crossing. Pilgrim Baptist's own printed history sets the raft account beside a second one, in which the family came up from St. Louis aboard the Northerner like everyone else on it, and says both versions have been handed down.

It does not argue about the paperwork.

The lot on Sibley Street cost two hundred dollars and was bought in another congregation's name. The call printed for January 1, 1869 carries his name second on a list of eighteen. The pulpit of the church he assembled belonged to other men for eleven years.

Nothing he said in any of those rooms was written down.

text:
🐱⚔️ THE LEGEND OF THE CAT SWORD IMMORTAL
Chapter 9 — FINAL CHAPTER
TEN THOUSAND FISH RETURN TO ONE 🐟✨

Every legend begins somewhere.

Some begin with a prophecy.

Some begin with a war.

Some begin when a hero draws a legendary sword.

But this one?

This one began with a tiny stray kitten staring at the sky and wondering...

"If ten thousand swords can fly, why can't dried fish?"

And now, after nine chapters, our little swordsman has finally come home.

🐟 The Hero's Reward

Morning returned to Qinghe Village.

The black tide was gone.

The people were safe.

And the kitten who had summoned ten thousand fish-shaped swords to save them...

Was currently buried beneath a mountain of dried fish.

"MEEEEOW!!!" ❤️

The villagers had prepared a feast for their tiny hero.

Grilled fish.

Fresh fish.

Dried fish.

More dried fish.

And even more dried fish.

The kitten stared at the enormous pile.

It had survived a monster army.

Witnessed the power of its future self.

And briefly become a genuine sword immortal.

But this...

THIS WAS THE GREATEST MIRACLE OF ALL. 🤣

Beside it, Songguo the squirrel sat before a mountain of nuts and pinecones.

"Squeak..."

So this was what being a hero felt like.

Interesting.

Very interesting.

🐿️ A Sword Repaired by Friendship

After the celebration, the kitten looked down at its broken bamboo sword.

It had been a gift from an old martial arts master in Xuanfang City.

A simple weapon.

Nothing legendary.

Yet it had accompanied the kitten through every step of its journey.

And now, it lay in two pieces.

"...Meow."

Songguo noticed.

Without a word, the squirrel gathered the broken pieces and disappeared into the village workshop.

There were strange noises.

Hammering.

Scraping.

A few unfortunate accidents.

And one particularly loud—

"SQUEEEEEAK!!!"

The kitten rushed inside.

Its disciple was hanging upside down from a vine.

Again.

"...Meow." 😭

After a rescue and several more attempts, Songguo finally presented its masterpiece.

A repaired bamboo sword.

Reinforced with small metal rings.

Its handle decorated with a tiny pinecone emblem.

It wasn't perfect.

It wasn't particularly elegant.

But it was strong.

The kitten gently swung it.

Whoosh.

The blade held.

It looked at Songguo.

Then softly patted the squirrel's head.

"Meow."

Thank you.

Songguo puffed out its chest.

"Squeak!"

Of course!

One studied the sword.

The other studied the world around it.

And somehow...

They had become exactly the companions each other needed.

🔥 Somewhere in Jinzhou, Changli Smiled

Several days later, a strange military report arrived in Jinzhou.

It described the destruction of an enormous Tacet Discord army near Qinghe Village.

The report included an unusual detail.

"The mysterious sword immortal appears to have been a tabby kitten."

The officials were confused.

Some thought the witnesses had been mistaken.

Others suspected the soldiers had written their report incorrectly.

But when the document reached Changli...

She stopped reading.

"Red scarf. Crimson feather ornament."

Her eyes softened.

"...So it was you."

She remembered a tiny kitten beneath a maple tree.

A kitten that could barely hold its bamboo sword.

A kitten that once struggled to move a single fallen leaf.

Now, according to the report...

It had commanded a celestial river of fish-shaped sword lights.

Changli smiled.

"So..."

"You really did it?"

She knew the kitten could not have reached such heights through ordinary training in only a few days.

Something extraordinary must have happened.

But for now, one thing mattered more.

The little one was alive.

She picked up her brush and added a note to the report.

"If the red-scarfed kitten is found, do not disturb it."

Then, after a moment's thought...

She added another line.

"Dried fish may be provided." ❤️

🏠 The Road Back to Xuanfang City

When the mountain roads reopened, the kitten and Songguo said goodbye to Qinghe Village.

The villagers offered food, supplies, and heartfelt thanks.

The village elder asked where they intended to go.

South led toward Jinzhou.

East led back to Xuanfang City.

The kitten looked east.

It remembered the fish shop.

The martial arts school.

The streets where it had once been a hungry stray.

Then it raised one paw.

"Meow."

Home.

Songguo hugged its pinecone.

"Squeak!"

Then home it is!

And so the two little travelers set off together.

🐱 Some Things Never Change

Xuanfang City looked exactly as the kitten remembered.

Busy streets.

Food stalls.

Merchants shouting.

Children laughing.

And, of course...

The familiar fish shop.

Old Wang was sitting outside, sorting dried fish.

He sighed.

"Things have been unusually quiet lately."

"That little fish thief hasn't shown up in ages..."

Then—

"Meow!"

Old Wang looked up.

A tabby kitten stood at the end of the street.

Red scarf.

Bamboo sword.

A squirrel beside it.

The old fish merchant stared.

"...YOU?!"

The kitten proudly raised its head.

"MEOW!"

I HAVE RETURNED!

Old Wang slowly stood.

"YOU LITTLE THIEF!"

"YOU STILL OWE ME HALF A DRIED FISH!"

The kitten froze.

"...Meow?"

The broom appeared.

"GET BACK HERE!!!"

"MEEEEEOOOOW!!!" 😭

The legendary Cat Sword Immortal fled through the streets.

Old Wang chased after it.

Songguo followed in complete disbelief.

"SQUEAK?!"

MASTER?!

DIDN'T YOU JUST DEFEAT AN ENTIRE ARMY?!

Apparently...

Defeating an army was easier than escaping an angry fish merchant.

⚔️ The Master Who Gave It a Sword

The kitten eventually escaped into the old martial arts school.

There, it met the white-bearded master who had once given it its first bamboo sword.

The old man recognized it immediately.

"Well, well."

"So you've returned."

The kitten bowed respectfully.

"Meow."

The master smiled.

"How has your swordsmanship progressed?"

The kitten stepped into the courtyard.

It planted its paws.

Balanced its tail.

And drew its repaired bamboo sword.

One swing.

Whoosh.

Three fallen leaves rose gently into the air.

They turned.

Floated.

Then settled back onto the ground.

The old master watched.

Then laughed.

"Wonderful!"

"You're finally beginning to understand the sword!"

The kitten's tail rose proudly.

"Meow!"

It didn't summon ten thousand fish.

It couldn't.

The borrowed power had returned to the future.

Instead, it showed the old master what it had truly learned.

Three fallen leaves, lifted by its own sword.

And that was enough to make the old man smile.

"Keep practicing, little one."

"Perhaps one day..."

"You really will become a sword immortal."

The kitten nodded.

"MEOW!"

I WILL!

🌅 The Sword Immortal Who Started It All

That evening, the kitten and Songguo sat upon the city walls.

The sky glowed with sunset.

Then suddenly—

A familiar voice echoed across Xuanfang City.

"SWORDS, COME."

The kitten looked up.

Its eyes widened.

Thousands of swords rose into the heavens.

Silver light filled the sky.

And there, standing beneath the sunset...

Was Qingxiao.

The white-haired sword immortal.

The very person who had inspired the kitten's impossible dream.

The kitten stood motionless.

It remembered the first time it had seen her.

Back then, it had been a tiny stray.

A creature with no sword.

No master.

No companion.

Only a ridiculous dream about flying fish.

And now...

It had traveled through mountains.

Learned from Changli.

Found Songguo.

Protected a village.

Witnessed its own future.

And briefly commanded ten thousand fish.

The kitten drew its bamboo sword.

It did not imitate Qingxiao.

It did not call out to her.

It simply raised its sword.

And bowed.

Thank you.

Thank you for showing me that the sky was bigger than I ever imagined.

Far away, Qingxiao sensed a faint sword intent.

She turned.

Her gaze settled upon a tiny red-scarfed kitten on the city wall.

For a moment, she seemed surprised.

Then...

She smiled.

And gently nodded back.

A sword immortal...

Acknowledging another swordsman.

The kitten froze.

"...Meow?"

SHE SAW ME?!

SHE ACTUALLY SAW ME?!

A moment later, it was rolling around on the city wall in pure happiness.

"MEEEEOWWW!!!" ❤️

Songguo stared.

"...Squeak?"

Master, please maintain your dignity.

🌌 The Fool's Final Joke

That night, the kitten returned to the old wooden box beside the fish shop.

Old Wang claimed he didn't want the little thief around.

Yet somehow...

The box now contained a soft, clean blanket.

Beside it stood two small bowls.

One filled with dried fish.

The other with nuts.

The kitten curled up inside.

Songguo settled beside it.

And soon, both were fast asleep.

High above the city, a mysterious white-haired young man sat upon a rooftop.

He looked toward the wooden box.

And laughed softly.

"Heh."

"The Cat Sword Immortal of Ten Thousand Fish..."

"And you're still sleeping in a broken wooden box."

A faint thread of destiny appeared in his hand.

It stretched into a distant future.

There, a black-robed feline sword immortal stood among the stars.

Ten thousand fish-shaped sword lights flowed behind it.

The stranger studied that future.

Then looked back at the sleeping kitten.

"Well..."

"Let's see whether you actually make it there."

He turned to leave.

But after a few steps, he paused.

"Hmm."

"One last gift, perhaps?"

He snapped his fingers.

Snap.

No thunder.

No celestial phenomenon.

No rewriting of the universe.

Just one little dried fish...

Floating gently through the night.

It drifted into the wooden box.

And settled beside the sleeping kitten.

The stranger smiled.

"Much better."

Then he vanished.

🐟 One Inch

The next morning, the kitten woke up.

And discovered an unexpected dried fish beside its paw.

"...Meow?"

It looked around.

Then stared at the fish.

Its eyes began to sparkle.

Could it be...?

Had its powers returned?!

The kitten quickly placed the fish at the other end of the wooden box.

Stepped backward.

Raised its bamboo sword.

And declared:

"FISH, COME!"

Nothing happened.

"..."

Again.

"MEOW!"

Nothing.

Again.

Again.

Again.

The dried fish refused to move.

The kitten's ears drooped.

"...Meow."

The power from that extraordinary night was gone.

It was still an ordinary little kitten.

Then a breeze passed through the wooden box.

A fallen leaf drifted upward.

The kitten remembered Changli's words.

Don't imitate Qingxiao.

Don't imitate me.

You're a cat.

Walk a path only you can walk.

The kitten took a breath.

It stopped shouting.

Stopped trying to force the fish to move.

Instead...

It listened.

To the wind.

To the air.

To the tiny movements surrounding the dried fish.

It lifted its sword.

And gently swung.

Whoosh.

The dried fish trembled.

The kitten froze.

"...Meow?"

It tried again.

Whoosh.

The fish shifted.

Just a little.

Barely noticeable.

But it moved.

The kitten stared.

Then—

"MEEEEOW!!!"

It jumped with excitement!

And immediately struck its head against the wooden box.

THUNK!

"MEOWWW!" 😭

Songguo woke up in alarm.

"SQUEAK?!"

But the kitten was already trying again.

✨ The Smallest Miracle

Later that afternoon, the two companions sat beside a quiet stream outside Xuanfang City.

The kitten placed a dried fish upon a stone.

Stepped back.

Raised its bamboo sword.

And closed its eyes.

It remembered everything.

Qingxiao's ten thousand swords.

Changli's crimson phoenix.

Songguo's friendship.

The people of Qinghe Village.

The mysterious stranger who had offered to make its dream come true.

And the future self it had once touched across the river of time.

Then...

It opened its eyes.

And whispered:

"Fish, come."

A breeze passed over the stream.

The dried fish trembled.

Rose.

And floated...

One inch above the stone.

Just one inch.

No celestial river.

No ten thousand swords.

No overwhelming power.

No cheering crowd.

Just a single dried fish.

Floating in the afternoon sunlight.

The kitten stared.

It could hardly believe what it was seeing.

Then the fish fell.

Tap.

Back onto the stone.

For three heartbeats, the kitten remained perfectly still.

Then—

"MEEEEEEEEOOOOOW!!!" ❤️🐟

It leaped into the air!

Rolled across the grass!

Waved its bamboo sword!

And celebrated as though it had just conquered the heavens!

Songguo rushed over.

"SQUEAK?!"

The kitten pointed at the fish.

"MEOW! MEOW!"

Songguo understood.

The squirrel dropped its tools.

Ran toward its friend.

And together...

The two little creatures danced beneath the afternoon sun.

Because this time...

No one had mocked fate for the kitten.

No one had borrowed power from the future.

No mysterious stranger had performed a miracle.

That one inch...

Belonged entirely to the kitten.

🌠 Epilogue — The Dream That Was Never a Joke

Somewhere beyond time and destiny...

The white-haired stranger noticed a tiny light flickering among countless worlds.

He looked inside.

A little kitten was celebrating because it had made one dried fish float.

One inch.

The stranger stared.

Then laughed.

"Hahahaha..."

"Unbelievable."

"You've already witnessed ten thousand fish filling the heavens..."

"And you're this happy over one inch?"

He shook his head.

But his smile remained.

He looked toward the river of destiny he had once rewritten.

And noticed something new.

A tiny light had appeared within it.

Not something he had created.

Not something borrowed from the future.

Something the kitten had kindled through its own effort.

The stranger watched quietly.

Then smiled.

"I mocked fate."

"I mocked time."

"But you..."

"You never mocked your own dream."

And with that...

He turned away.

Leaving the little swordsman to walk its own path.

THE END 🐱⚔️🐟

Nine chapters.

One tiny kitten.

One loyal squirrel.

A bamboo sword.

A crimson feather.

A mysterious stranger.

And a dream that began with a ridiculous question.

If swords can fly, why can't dried fish?

Once, ten thousand fish answered the kitten's call.

But that was a miracle borrowed from the future.

Today, one dried fish rose an inch.

And that...

Was a miracle the kitten created for itself.

Ten Thousand Fish Return to One.

Not because the number ten thousand matters.

But because every extraordinary journey begins with one small step.

And sometimes...

The greatest sword immortal in the world is simply a little cat who refuses to stop dreaming. ❤️

Thank you for following this journey.

The Legend of the Cat Sword Immortal — Complete.

🐱⚔️🐟🐿️🌌

🐱⚔️ THE LEGEND OF THE CAT SWORD IMMORTAL
Volume I: The Path of the Sword
Chapter 7 — The Village Warning Bell 🔔

Two tiny travelers ran through the mountains at sunrise.

One was a tabby kitten wearing a red scarf, with a bamboo sword strapped to its back.

The other was a squirrel carrying an enormous pinecone.

Neither was particularly strong.

Neither could speak a single word of human language.

And neither had ever warned an entire village about an approaching army of monsters.

Unfortunately...

That was exactly what they needed to do.

🐱 Mission One: Make the Humans Understand

The village of Qinghe was peaceful.

Smoke rose from kitchen chimneys.

Farmers prepared for another ordinary day.

Two young guards stood at the entrance, discussing the previous night's rain.

Then—

"MEOW! MEOW! MEEEEOW!!!"

A tiny kitten came charging toward them.

It pointed north.

Drew its bamboo sword.

Waved it frantically.

Then pointed toward the village.

"MEOW!!!"

MONSTERS!

LOTS OF MONSTERS!

THEY'RE COMING THIS WAY!

The guards stared.

"...A cat?"

One crouched down.

"Oh, look! It has a little sword!"

The other laughed.

"Maybe it's performing tricks!"

The kitten froze.

"..."

It tried again.

It growled.

Waved its paws.

Pretended to attack an invisible monster.

"MEOWWWW!!!"

The guards burst into laughter.

"Hahaha! It thinks it's a tiger!"

The kitten's soul nearly left its body.

THE FATE OF AN ENTIRE VILLAGE WAS BEING MISTAKEN FOR A CAT PERFORMANCE. 😭

One guard even offered it a piece of bread.

The kitten stared at the bread.

It was hungry.

Very hungry.

But this was no time for breakfast!

It pushed the bread away.

"MEOW!!!"

The guard blinked.

"...Not hungry?"

The kitten looked ready to cry.

🐿️ Mission Two: Draw the Danger

Then the squirrel noticed something.

A wooden board.

Several pieces of charcoal.

And an opportunity.

"SQUEAK!"

It grabbed a piece of charcoal and began drawing.

A forest.

A village.

A crowd of dark monsters.

And an arrow pointing directly toward the village.

The kitten's eyes lit up.

"MEOW!"

Brilliant!

It grabbed another piece of charcoal.

And drew a heroic kitten standing in front of the village, holding a magnificent sword.

The squirrel examined the drawing.

Then quietly made the kitten smaller.

The kitten stared.

"...Meow?"

The squirrel made the monsters bigger.

"...MEOW?!"

Much bigger.

The heroic kitten was now barely a dot.

"MEEEOOOW!!!"

YOU ARE INSULTING YOUR MASTER!

The squirrel pointed toward the distant mountains.

"Squeak."

The kitten looked.

Far away, a dark tide was slowly spreading across the forest.

It looked back at the drawing.

Then silently put down the charcoal.

...

Fair enough.

The proportions were accurate.

🔔 The Forgotten Bell

The village elder finally understood their warning.

The northern forest had been unusually quiet.

Wild animals had fled south.

And now two frightened little creatures had arrived, desperately trying to warn everyone.

Something was wrong.

Very wrong.

The elder ordered the village guards to gather everyone.

But there was a problem.

In the center of Qinghe stood an old warning bell.

Long ago, its sound had alerted villagers to bandits and wild beasts.

Unfortunately, the wooden tower was rotting.

The rope had snapped.

And the striking hammer had disappeared years earlier.

No one could safely climb up to ring it.

The kitten looked at the bell.

Then at its bamboo sword.

Its eyes widened.

AN IDEA!

It remembered Changli's lessons.

The wind.

The fallen leaf.

That miraculous inch of movement.

The kitten planted all four paws firmly on the ground.

Raised its sword.

And swung!

"MEOW!!!"

Whoosh.

A tiny breeze passed through the bell tower.

The bell did not move.

Again!

"MEOW!!!"

Nothing.

Again!

Again!

Again!

Eventually, the kitten collapsed onto the ground.

Exhausted.

The bell remained silent.

It stared up at the enormous bronze structure.

For the first time that morning...

The little swordsman felt very, very small.

🌰 The Squirrel's First Invention

While the kitten rested, the squirrel studied the bell tower.

The branches.

The broken rope.

The wooden beams.

The stones scattered nearby.

Its eyes began to sparkle.

"SQUEAK!"

It gathered vines.

Found a wooden pole.

And started assembling a strange little mechanism.

The kitten watched in confusion.

"...Meow?"

The squirrel pulled a vine.

WHOOSH!

The pole shot upward!

THUNK!

It struck the wooden tower.

Not the bell.

Failure.

The squirrel adjusted the angle.

Tried again.

WHOOSH!

THUNK!

Missed.

Third attempt!

WHOOSH!

The pole flew completely off the mechanism.

And landed at the village elder's feet.

"..."

The elder stared at the two little animals.

The kitten slowly hid its bamboo sword behind its back.

The squirrel hugged its pinecone.

The elder sighed.

"Well... at least you're trying."

But the squirrel wasn't finished.

It rearranged the vines.

Changed the support.

Adjusted the direction of the wooden pole.

Then pointed at the kitten.

"SQUEAK!"

The kitten nodded.

"MEOW!"

Together, they pulled.

The vine tightened.

The pole swung.

And—

DONG!!!

The ancient bell rang.

Its deep voice rolled across the entire village.

Farmers stopped working.

Children looked up.

Birds scattered from the rooftops.

The elder turned in astonishment.

The kitten froze.

The squirrel froze.

Then—

"MEEEEOW!!!"

"SQUEEEEEAK!!!"

They jumped into each other's arms.

THEY DID IT!

THEY ACTUALLY DID IT!

Unfortunately...

The wooden pole rebounded.

THWACK!!!

Straight onto the kitten's head.

"MEOWWWWWW!!!" 😭

The squirrel panicked.

"SQUEAK?!"

The elder stared for a moment.

Then burst into laughter.

"Hahahaha!"

"What extraordinary little creatures!"

And so, with the villagers' help, the strange mechanism was secured.

The warning bell rang again.

And again.

And again.

DONG!

DONG!

DONG!

For the first time in many years...

Qinghe's warning bell had awakened.

⚔️ The Enemy Is Real

Villagers gathered in the square.

Some were frightened.

Some were skeptical.

Others believed the warning was an overreaction.

Until a hunter returned from the northern ridge.

His face was pale.

"Elder!"

"The northern pass..."

"There really are monsters!"

Everyone fell silent.

The hunter struggled to catch his breath.

"Tacet Discords."

"Dozens..."

"No..."

"Hundreds..."

He looked back toward the mountains.

His voice trembled.

"I couldn't count them all."

The village elder closed his eyes.

The warning had been real.

And the danger was much closer than anyone imagined.

🌑 The Road That Washed Away

The villagers began preparing to evacuate.

Families gathered food.

Parents carried their children.

Farmers loaded their carts.

But the previous night's storm had destroyed part of the southern mountain road.

The carts couldn't pass.

The elderly couldn't safely cross.

And there wasn't enough time to repair the route.

The elder looked toward the northern entrance.

Then made his decision.

"Send out everyone who can leave."

"The rest of us..."

He paused.

"...will defend the village."

A young guard protested.

"With what?!"

"We barely have a dozen hunters!"

"Those things are Tacet Discords!"

The elder said nothing.

Because he had no answer.

The kitten stood quietly behind the crowd.

It didn't understand every word.

But it understood fear.

It saw parents holding their children.

Old people staring at the mountains.

A little girl clinging to her mother's clothes.

"Mom..."

"Will our home disappear?"

Her mother hugged her tightly.

"No, sweetheart."

But her voice was shaking.

The kitten watched.

And remembered something.

Long ago, in Xuanfang City, it had slept inside a broken wooden box behind a fish shop.

It knew what it meant to have almost nothing.

It knew what it meant to be afraid of losing even that.

Slowly, the kitten looked down at its bamboo sword.

"...Meow."

🐱 The First Sword Drawn for Someone Else

By sunset, the village had prepared its defenses.

Wooden stakes.

Stone barricades.

Hunting bows.

Farm tools sharpened into makeshift weapons.

The squirrel hurried between the villagers, helping build simple traps and warning mechanisms.

Some worked.

Some didn't.

One accidentally left the squirrel dangling upside down from a branch.

"SQUEAK!!!" 😭

The kitten had to rescue it.

"Meow!"

Then, as the sun disappeared behind the mountains...

A low rumble came from the north.

Rrrrrrr...

The trees shook.

Birds erupted from the forest.

A guard raised his bow.

"They're here..."

One twisted creature emerged from the darkness.

Then another.

And another.

Ten.

Twenty.

Fifty.

Behind them...

The forest itself seemed to move.

A black tide stretched across the mountainside.

The kitten stood beside the wooden barricade.

Its paws were trembling.

It was afraid.

Terribly afraid.

It remembered Qingxiao.

The white-haired sword immortal who had once commanded ten thousand swords beneath the heavens.

It remembered Changli.

The crimson-haired swordswoman whose phoenix had illuminated the night.

But Qingxiao wasn't here.

Changli wasn't here.

There were no ten thousand swords.

No crimson phoenix.

No miraculous power.

Just a tiny kitten.

A fragile bamboo sword.

And a red scarf bearing a single crimson feather.

The kitten looked back at the village.

At the children.

At the elderly.

At the guards who had laughed at its warning.

At the little girl who was afraid of losing her home.

Then it stepped forward.

Past the barricade.

Past the guards.

Toward the approaching monsters.

It drew its bamboo sword.

"...Meow."

Once, it had wanted to learn swordsmanship for one simple reason.

It wanted dried fish to fly.

But now...

For the first time...

It wanted its sword to protect someone.

The squirrel stood behind it.

Its fluffy tail trembled.

It looked at the approaching army.

Then at its friend.

For a moment, it seemed ready to run.

Instead, it picked up a little wooden stick.

And stepped beside the kitten.

"...Squeak."

The kitten turned.

The squirrel nodded.

They faced the darkness together.

A bamboo sword.

A wooden stick.

Two very small creatures.

Against an army.

The first Tacet Discord charged.

The kitten lowered its stance.

Remembered Changli's teachings.

And leaped forward.

"MEEEEOOOW!!!"

Its first real battle had begun.

✨ Somewhere Beyond Time

Far away...

In a place where direction had no meaning...

Where countless lights drifted like stars...

Each tiny point reflected a different story.

A kingdom rising.

A civilization falling.

A hero being born.

A world approaching its end.

Among those countless lights was one particularly small.

Almost insignificant.

Within it, a tiny kitten raised a bamboo sword against an overwhelming tide of monsters.

For a brief moment...

The light flickered.

Then—

A faint chuckle echoed through the endless stillness.

"...Heh."

Nothing more.

No divine intervention.

No miraculous rescue.

No power descending from the heavens.

The village's fate remained in the hands of those fighting to protect it.

But among the countless stories drifting through that strange place...

One little light had stopped moving.

As though something...

Or someone...

Had become interested.

END OF CHAPTER 7

Next Chapter: Chapter 8 — The Bamboo Sword and the Black Tide

A kitten who wanted flying fish.

A squirrel who wanted to build things.

A village that almost ignored their warning.

And an ancient bell that finally rang because two little creatures refused to give up.

Their journey began with a dream.

But today, that dream has led them somewhere neither expected.

To the front line of a battle they cannot possibly win alone.

And somewhere beyond the reach of ordinary eyes...

Their story has gained its first mysterious spectator. 🌌

🐱⚔️🐿️🔔

text:
🐱⚔️ THE LEGEND OF THE CAT SWORD IMMORTAL
Volume I: The Path of the Sword
Chapter 6 — The Little Follower on the Mountain Road 🐿️

The morning after Changli's departure, a tiny kitten set out into the world.

A bamboo sword rested on its back.

A red scarf fluttered around its neck.

And a little crimson feather, a farewell gift from Changli, swayed gently in the breeze.

"MEOW!"

THE MARTIAL WORLD AWAITS!

The kitten marched proudly down the mountain trail.

It had barely taken ten steps when—

Rustle...

Something moved behind it.

The kitten froze.

"...Meow?"

Rustle... rustle...

It slowly drew its bamboo sword.

Could it be?!

Its very first encounter with a mountain bandit?!

The kitten raised its sword dramatically.

"MEOW!!!"

SHOW YOURSELF, VILLAIN!

Two tiny eyes appeared between the bushes.

Then a fluffy little head emerged.

"...Squeak?"

A squirrel.

A very small squirrel.

Carrying a pinecone almost as large as its own head.

The kitten stared.

The squirrel stared back.

"...Meow."

Oh.

Not a bandit.

Just a pinecone merchant.

🐟 The First Business Deal

The squirrel sniffed the kitten's backpack.

"Squeak!"

The kitten looked at the squirrel's pinecone.

Then at its own dried fish.

A realization struck.

A TRADE!

Its first commercial transaction in the martial world!

The kitten carefully placed a dried fish on a stone.

The squirrel placed its pinecone beside it.

They exchanged goods.

Both looked delighted.

Until—

The squirrel bit the dried fish.

"..."

The kitten tried biting the pinecone.

"..."

They slowly looked at each other.

Then at their food.

Then at each other again.

Without a word, they exchanged everything back.

The kitten happily ate its fish.

The squirrel hugged its pinecone.

THE FIRST BUSINESS DEAL OF THE CAT SWORD IMMORTAL...

WAS A COMPLETE FAILURE. 🤣

🐿️ The First Disciple

The kitten waved goodbye and continued walking.

Ten steps later—

Rustle.

The squirrel was following it.

Twenty steps later—

Rustle rustle.

Still following.

The kitten stopped.

"Meow?"

The squirrel nodded enthusiastically.

"Squeak!"

The kitten pointed at itself.

"Meow?"

You want to follow ME?

"SQUEAK!"

The kitten stood a little taller.

Of course!

Its magnificent sword aura must have inspired admiration!

Even in these remote mountains, someone had recognized its extraordinary potential!

The kitten nodded solemnly.

"MEOW!"

VERY WELL!

FROM THIS DAY FORWARD, YOU SHALL BE MY FIRST DISCIPLE!

The squirrel bounced happily.

"Squeak squeak!"

Whether it actually wanted to learn swordsmanship...

Or simply thought the kitten had more snacks...

Remained a mystery.

⚔️ The Dangers of Teaching

The kitten decided that its new disciple needed immediate training.

It drew its bamboo sword.

Raised it proudly.

And swung.

WHOOSH!

A fallen leaf fluttered into the air.

"MEOW!"

BEHOLD!

THE SUPREME SWORD ART!

The squirrel watched with enormous eyes.

"SQUEAK!"

It rushed over to a tree, picked up a little branch, and began copying the kitten.

"Squeak!"

SWISH!

Nothing happened.

"SQUEAK!"

SWISH!

Still nothing.

The squirrel grew frustrated.

It swung with all its might.

THWACK!!!

The branch struck the kitten directly on the head.

"..."

The kitten froze.

The squirrel froze.

Then—

"MEEEEOOOOWWWW!!!" 😭

The kitten collapsed, clutching its head.

The squirrel panicked and rushed over to comfort its master.

The kitten looked at its new disciple with tears in its eyes.

It had learned something important.

BEING A MASTER WAS MUCH MORE DANGEROUS THAN EXPECTED.

🌧️ Two Little Travelers

That afternoon, heavy rain swept across the mountains.

The kitten and squirrel found shelter inside a small cave.

Outside, thunder rolled across the forest.

The squirrel curled up with its pinecone.

The kitten sat near the entrance, staring at the rain.

It remembered Changli.

The warm campfire.

The maple tree.

Her gentle voice.

"You are a cat."

"So walk a path that only you can walk."

The kitten lowered its head.

"...Meow."

The squirrel noticed.

It quietly pushed its precious pinecone toward the kitten.

"Squeak?"

The kitten blinked.

Then took a dried fish from its backpack and offered it in return.

Both stared at the food.

Both remembered their disastrous first trade.

And both pushed their own food back.

"..."

Then they sat beside each other, watching the rain.

Neither understood the other's language.

But somehow...

The mountain no longer felt quite so lonely. ❤️

🌙 The Wounded Traveler

Late that night, the kitten heard footsteps.

Slow.

Heavy.

Uneven.

A wounded traveler staggered along the muddy road.

His clothes were torn.

Blood stained his shoulder.

A broken sword hung from his hand.

He stumbled.

Then collapsed.

"The Tacet..."

"They're moving south..."

"Someone..."

"Someone must warn the village..."

His voice faded.

The kitten hurried outside.

"Meow?"

It gently touched the man's hand.

No response.

It pushed against his arm.

Nothing.

It tried again.

And again.

But the traveler was far too heavy.

The kitten sat helplessly in the rain.

It looked down at its tiny paws.

If Changli were here, she could save him.

If Qingxiao were here, perhaps one sword would be enough.

But neither of them was here.

There was only a kitten.

A kitten whose bamboo sword was still fragile.

A kitten that couldn't even summon one dried fish.

For a moment, it didn't know what to do.

Then it remembered something Changli had taught it.

"Don't just look at the fish."

"Look at the water."

The kitten suddenly turned and ran back into the cave.

"MEOW! MEOW!"

The squirrel woke up.

"Squeak?"

The kitten pointed outside.

Together, they rushed to the wounded traveler.

They tried pushing.

Pulling.

Dragging.

After enormous effort...

The man moved half an inch.

Both collapsed from exhaustion.

"...Meow."

"...Squeak."

Then the squirrel noticed some vines and fallen branches nearby.

Its eyes lit up.

"SQUEAK!"

It began gathering materials.

The kitten watched.

Then understood.

They couldn't move the man with strength alone.

But perhaps they could use the things around them.

They pulled vines.

Levered branches.

Used the slope of the ground.

And slowly...

Very slowly...

Moved the traveler toward shelter.

One inch.

Then another.

Then another.

By dawn, they had finally dragged him into the cave.

The kitten collapsed on its back.

The squirrel fell asleep hugging its tail.

Neither had any strength left.

But the wounded traveler was safe from the rain.

For the first time, the kitten had saved someone without using its sword.

🌄 The Black Tide

At sunrise, the traveler regained consciousness.

He looked around.

A tiny squirrel slept beside him.

A kitten with a bamboo sword sat near the cave entrance.

"...You two?"

The kitten turned.

"Meow!"

Suddenly, the traveler remembered.

His face turned pale.

"The village!"

"Someone must warn the village!"

He struggled to stand but collapsed again.

"The Tacet aren't wandering randomly..."

"Something is driving them..."

"The entire northern forest..."

His voice trembled.

"It's being swallowed."

The kitten followed his gaze.

Far beyond the mountains, a dark line stretched across the horizon.

At first, it looked like a distant storm.

But it was moving.

Slowly.

Relentlessly.

And directly toward a peaceful little village.

The kitten stared.

"...Meow?"

It didn't know what the darkness was.

It didn't understand the scale of the danger.

But it understood one thing.

There were people ahead who didn't know what was coming.

The kitten looked at its bamboo sword.

Then at its tiny paws.

It wasn't strong enough to defeat an army.

It wasn't even strong enough to carry one injured human.

But perhaps...

It could still do something.

It turned toward the squirrel.

"Meow."

The squirrel blinked.

"Squeak?"

The kitten pointed toward the village.

The squirrel looked at the distant black tide.

Then back at its friend.

For a moment, it hesitated.

Finally, it picked up its pinecone.

And stood beside the kitten.

"SQUEAK!"

We'll go together.

Two tiny figures stepped out of the cave.

One carried a bamboo sword.

The other carried a pinecone.

Neither was a hero.

Neither possessed extraordinary power.

Neither knew what awaited them.

But they began running toward the village.

Because sometimes...

You don't need to be strong enough to defeat the danger.

You just need to be brave enough to warn someone it's coming.

END OF CHAPTER 6

Next Chapter: Chapter 7 — The Village Warning Bell 🔔

The little kitten still dreams of commanding ten thousand flying fish.

But for now, it has something far more important to do.

Save the people who don't know the darkness is coming.

And somewhere beyond the mountains...

The black tide continues to advance.

🐱⚔️🐿️

EUROPEAN THREAT IMPLICATIONS

Iranian external operations have repeatedly used criminal intermediaries because criminals offer access, plausible deniability and disposable manpower. 

Previous European cases have involved surveillance, intimidation, assassination planning, arson and targeting of Iranian dissidents, Jewish institutions and Israeli interests. 

Fairford adds Western military infrastructure to the immediate threat set.

Priority exposure now includes:

US and allied airbases supporting operations against Iran.

Fuel, maintenance, transport and accommodation supporting deployed forces.

Defence contractors and civilian suppliers with predictable routines.

Naval port visits and replenishment activity.

Iranian dissidents and Persian-language media.

Israeli diplomatic, commercial and community targets.

Jewish institutions.

Energy, telecommunications and transport systems suitable for disruptive attacks.

This is not a uniform European threat increase. 

Facilities directly supporting operations against Iran, or whose routines are publicly observable, face greater exposure than unrelated sites.

European riots remain predominantly domestic events. 

There is still no public evidence that Tehran commanded the French or Dutch disorder. 

Iranian-aligned actors can nevertheless amplify unrest, circulate divisive narratives, display proxy symbolism and draw police and intelligence resources away from protective-security tasks. 

Exploitation is plausible; orchestration remains unproven.

YEMEN/SAUDI ARABIA/UK

Britain is deploying Typhoons, an A400M and advisers to Saudi Arabia for defensive counter-air missions. 

Voyager refuelling support continues. 

London says its aircraft will not conduct offensive strikes in Yemen.

The selected box is limited air defence. 

Its possible contents include UK aircraft engaging Houthi missiles or UAS, dependence on Saudi identification and targeting systems, increased exposure of British personnel and eventual pressure to strike launch infrastructure.

The reported death toll from the Houthi strike on the Shabwa camp has reached at least 73, with more than 200 wounded.

Direct liaison reporting states that Saudi Special Forces were inside the camp. 

This has not been confirmed publicly. If accurate, Shabwa represents a direct strike on Saudi personnel and substantially increases the probability of retaliation.

Saudi and Emirati support for Yemeni government forces is intended to restore pressure without recreating the previous large intervention. 

The danger is that funding, advisers, Special Forces and air cover recreate strategic ownership without providing the force density or political settlement necessary to win.

HORMUZ/MARITIME PRESSURE

Iran continues to exploit uncertainty around Hormuz. 

Claims that tankers struck mines remain insufficiently corroborated by independent maritime authorities.

The claim itself still creates effect. Shipowners, crews and insurers must react before attribution is resolved. 

Iran can therefore impose costs without formally closing the Strait or accepting responsibility for every incident.

The decisive escalation threshold would be a verified mine strike causing mass casualties, a major spill or the loss of a high-value vessel. 

Such an event could turn protective escorts into active mine-clearing and counterforce operations.

NEGOTIATIONS

Pakistan and Qatar are attempting to preserve mediation channels. 

Oil prices responded to the Pakistani army chief’s meeting with the Iranian president, demonstrating the market value of even limited diplomatic movement.

Washington believes it may be selecting an off-ramp. 

Tehran may believe it is selecting time: delay until the US midterms, create divisions between partners, reduce economic pressure and preserve remaining military capability.

Talks remain useful, but talks conducted while every side improves its position are escalation management, not peace.

Today, as I wrap up my 50-state mowing tour for Breast Cancer Awareness Month here in Hawaii, my heart is filled with emotions that are hard to put into words. Over the past three weeks, I’ve traveled across America, mowing lawns and sitting down with incredible women whose lives have been forever changed by breast cancer. I’ve met people currently fighting for their lives, survivors who have overcome unimaginable challenges, and families carrying the heartbreaking pain of losing someone they love. I’ve listened to stories of fear, courage, faith, heartbreak, and hope. There were moments when we laughed together, moments when tears were shed, and moments when I simply sat there in silence, trying to find the right words. Every person I met reminded me that behind every cancer diagnosis is a human being with a family, dreams, memories, and a story that deserves to be heard. I may have traveled 50 states to mow lawns, but I go home with something far greater than I ever imagined, stories and memories that will stay with me for the rest of my life. ❤️

To every person who opened their home, shared their journey, shed a tear, offered a hug, or trusted me with the memory of someone they lost, THANK YOU. You are the reason I made this journey. To everyone who helped me find families, followed along, prayed for me, or supported this mission in any way, thank you from the bottom of my heart. My hope is that these stories will encourage someone to schedule that mammogram, remind someone battling cancer that they are not alone, and inspire all of us to appreciate the precious gift of another day. This tour may be over, but the stories I’ve heard and the people I’ve met will forever be a part of me. Fifty states may have been the goal, but touching even one life was always the purpose. And if one person finds hope, courage, or the strength to keep going because of these stories, then every mile was worth it. MISSION COMPLETE.

text:
Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.
