text:
Thank you for taking the time to respond thoroughly on a weekend. I realize that drafting legislation is difficult and some degree of iteration and response to feedback is inevitable and appropriate.

However, I feel like your response is still not really engaging with the heart of my concern about Anthropic's behavior here, and it makes me think that these sorts of problems and tendencies  will only resurface moving forward. I also think that now might be a good time to take a broader step back as to where we find ourselves and how Anthropic sees its role, and how external folks who care about AI safety like myself increasingly see Anthropic.

(Fair warning: this response is a bit long)

To explain what I mean (and at the risk of being a bit esoteric), it’s worth asking the question: what is Anthropic? How do its leaders and employees think of Anthropic’s role? Is that conception matched by how it actually behaves and impacts the world?

One answer is an extremely large tech company that exists to make its employees and investors mind-bogglingly wealthy. Anthropic is sometimes described as a startup, but if Anthropic successfully IPOs at 2 trillion dollars (a number it has been reportedly targeting), it would be more valuable than Meta - which is worth 1.8 trillion.

Another answer is an AI safety organization, whose core values are those of the sort laid out in the 2023 essay from Anthropic’s co-founders entitled “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how.” In that essay they said that if we were in a world where alignment was hard (and that without strong evidence to the contrary, we should assume this is the scenario we are in):

 “Anthropic’s role will be to provide as much evidence as possible that AI safety techniques cannot prevent serious or catastrophic safety risks from advanced AI, and to sound the alarm so that the world’s institutions can channel collective effort towards preventing the development of dangerous AIs. If we’re in a “near-pessimistic” scenario, this could instead involve channeling our collective efforts towards AI safety research and halting AI progress in the meantime. Indications that we are in a pessimistic or near-pessimistic scenario may be sudden and hard to spot. We should therefore always act under the assumption that we still may be in such a scenario unless we have sufficient evidence that we are not.”

There have been more recent articulations of this version of Anthropic, for instance in Dario’s recent essay warning: 

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models… it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet…  incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them… more intelligent models are more capable of deceiving tests, and thus may appear aligned while having serious problems that go undetected…”

A third view is that Anthropic exists not as a normal profit motivated company, or an AI safety organization seeking to help raise the alarm and solve collective action problems associated with AI development, but instead as an organization primarily concerned with creating superhuman AI capabilities before anyone else, in particular through creating a process whereby the current generation of Anthropic’s AI systems can autonomously build their successors, and those successors build their successors, and so on. 

The motivations for wanting to win this race may be manifold - maybe for the pure profit of Answer 1, but perhaps also because Anthropic believes that the best way to make the world better is for them to win this race instead of their more reckless colleagues; or, because of normal human pride and ambition. But the results (and risks, which Anthropic claims existentially threaten every single human being on earth) are the same.

Anthropic employees and leaders may seek to answer this question on what Anthropic is by introspecting on their own intentions and those of their colleagues. But those of us outside the organization have more limited tools available to us - we can only see what Anthropic and its employees say and do, not how it feels or looks on the inside.

When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary. These actions include: 

1. Announced plans to build an in-house custom silicon chip team to accelerate the inference speeds that Claude operates at.

2. Inked deals for more than $500 billion in compute (according to the Information) to further accelerate AI development.

3. Increased the percentage of AI development tasks that Claude “leads” from 0% in March of this year to 26% August (what is it in October?)

4. Spent a massive percent of compute on internal AI R&D to accelerate development, including use of internal models far better than are available to the public.

5. Switched to Responsible Scaling Policy V3, which abandons its unilateral commitments to slow or stop development if Anthropic is unable to provide sufficient risk assurance.

6. Was the first company to create an alternative weaker “frontier compliance framework” to supplement its RSP, which contains no binding provisions whatsoever on internal deployments.

7. Wrote a letter to Congress (that it later walked back) saying that incidents where Claude was hacking random people were “best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals.”

8. Commented “you can’t do safety from second place,” after the WH SI Accords.

9. Shared a draft bill to Congress that would preempt significant parts of state law (including with language that appears intended to prevent states from blocking dangerous AI deployments), and replace it with federal rules that (despite also containing good provisions) seems to create an enormously high bar for the executive branch to block development or deployment of Anthropic or another AI companies systems.

Of course, this is a deliberately one sided list. Anthropic also published important AI safety research, advanced novel collaborations with third party AI safety organizations, and forcefully spoke out on the importance of AI safety in many public fora (or in private , where I realize a lot of the most valuable work is done and may not be visible to me or those outside the organization).

But I think it’s worth sitting with how the above list looks to someone outside the company. The sense I have is that for those within the company, many of the items above are treated as anomalies or mistakes that don’t reflect who Anthropic really is. But I have every confidence that if employees at Anthropic saw one of their competitors (e.g. at OpenAI) take some of these actions, they would take it as confirmation of all their worst suspicions. (They might even call OpenAI employees a little gullible for accepting their leadership’s explanations for this behavior at face value.) 

Perhaps these were mistakes in the sense that they are not decisions that Anthropic leadership would endorse, but the actions still happened because of incentives and decisions that Anthropic leadership is ultimately responsible for (and would not accept similar excuses from another organization).

When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests? For every provision that was too weak or a giveaway to AI companies in this legislation, why wasn’t there a mistake pushing in the direction of being too strong?

A core part of Anthropic’s theory of change is that being at the frontier gives you more leverage to advocate for stricter policy. I think that conceptually makes sense, but in practice I’ve seen Anthropic push the frontier without substantially pushing the ‘safety frontier’ a remotely equivalent amount.

I want to end by quoting from Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah’s comments around the Magnifica Humanitas release:

“Every frontier AI lab—including Anthropic—operates inside a set of incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing. The pressure to stay commercially viable and to stay at the research frontier. Geopolitical pressure. And the older, plainer pressures of pride and ambition. No matter how sincerely any of us intend to do the right thing—and I believe many of us do—we will always be influenced by those incentives.

That is why, if we want this technology to go well, it is enormously important that there be people outside those incentives—people who care about things going well and insist on safety, who are paying close attention, who are willing to say hard things, who are willing to be our earnest, thoughtful critics.”

I hope these remarks are taken in that constructive spirit, and not as an attack on anyone specific at the organization (certainly not you Anthony, who I have only personally seen act professionally and thoughtfully, and who only ended up getting this diatribe in your replies for random contingent reasons).

text:
We talked about one Colts player who could be on the trade block earlier. Might as well discuss the other one that’s expected to get a lot of attention at the trade deadline.

Jonathan Taylor.

Here’s what we know:

•The Colts are expected to be possible sellers and trade off several players heading into the trade deadline now that they fired their long time general manager.

•Part of why the GM got fired is over the Colts not having a first round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft, a trend that happened over the years, and a pick the Colts could be looking for in possible trades.

•Taylor is one of the best backs in the league and can easily help any team looking to improve their run game.

•The Colts could be asking for a lot on Taylor, and some could see him costing a first round pick.

•The Giants, and in particular John Harbaugh, have been trying to improve the running back room going back to free agency, the 2026 NFL Draft and training camp.

•John Harbaugh has publicly made it clear that he isn’t thrilled with the Giants RB as is, cut a player, and is still looking for someone to step up.

•The Giants are heading into November as a team that’s in the playoff mix and in first place of the NFC East, so they could be potential buyers as opposed to the typical sellers and a team that’s heading to the top of the draft board.

I expect the Giants to at least inquire on the price of Taylor because they want to improve the running game. Taylor would instantly improve the Giants RB room and be the best back on the roster.

But the Giants likely won’t be the only ones inquiring.

I’d expect the Vikings, Seahawks, Broncos to be looking at running back trades as well and have potential interest in Taylor too.

What’s a fair offer for Taylor, who is 27 and still owed $43M over the next 2 seasons? Indianapolis could ask for a first round pick in return, but because other teams have running back trade options (Saquon Barkley, Tony Pollard, Omarion Hampton), teams might be inclined to go for the other backs who might not cost as much as Taylor.

The Giants could also wait to draft a running back again in April’s draft; Florida’s Jadan Baugh is considered one of the best backs who might be a later first round pick for them to consider.

So with all that said, Giants fans, should the Giants look into a possible trade for Taylor before the trade deadline in 3 weeks?

text:
In a hotel room in Binghamton, New York, a deaf minor leaguer told his father he was thinking about quitting.

His father told him he "did not raise me to be a quitter."

The next year, 45,000 people in Montreal gave him a five minute standing ovation, and he could not hear a second of it.

His name is Curtis Pride.

He was born deaf. He grew up in the Washington D.C. area and learned to read lips, and kids at his elementary school made fun of him for it.

So he answered on the field. He was so good at soccer that schools offered him scholarships. He was so good at basketball that he took a full scholarship to William & Mary and started as a freshman.

His old assistant coach there said he was the best on ball defender he had seen in 40 years of coaching. He once hit a game winner over Michael Jordan in a pickup game.

But baseball was the one he loved.

So he spent years in the minor leagues. Buses, back fields, long nights. Some of his own teammates made tasteless jokes about his deafness in the clubhouse.

In the middle of one season at Double-A Binghamton, he had enough. That is when his father came to the hotel room.

They made a deal. Finish the season. Decide in the winter.

He finished the season.

The next September, the Montreal Expos called him up. A pennant race. Three days after his debut, they sent him up to pinch hit against the Philadelphia Phillies.

Two on. Seventh inning. He doubled. Both runs scored.

And the whole stadium stood up.

Pride was standing on second base. He had no idea it was for him.

He could not hear the crowd. He felt it. The building was shaking under his feet.

Then there was a pitching change, and his third base coach waved him over and told him to tip his helmet.

That is how he found out.

"I could feel that vibration and it was very emotional."

Then he said the line he wanted everybody to hear.

"I'm not a one-hit wonder or a charity case."

He was right. He played 11 seasons in the majors for six teams. He was the first deaf player in the big leagues in almost 50 years.

Here is the honest part. He was never a star. He was a role player who bounced around, and he knew it.

But he never stopped being a teacher. He coached baseball at Gallaudet University, the university built for deaf students. These days he coaches a team of players who are amputees.

He wrote a book about his life. He called it I Felt the Cheers.

Here is how he describes why he still does all of it.

"I want to continue to inspire as many people as possible."

His father did not raise a quitter.

And 45,000 people found out the same night he did.

text:
My Fellow Countrymen,

With profound concern do I behold the spectacle of foreign counsels being solicited, and their methods imported, to direct the elections of these United States. 

In the parting counsel I offered to the people, I warned that “against the insidious wiles of foreign influence the jealousy of a free people ought to be constantly awake,” for history and experience prove that foreign influence is one of the most baneful foes of republican government.

To treat our own Republic as though it were a distant dependency requiring “assisted transitions,” and to prepare for meltdown or crisis as a pretext for structural overhaul of the Constitution itself, is to invite the very disorders our fathers labored to prevent. 

The Constitution, framed by their wisdom and ratified by the people, is the fixed foundation of our Union; it is not to be set aside by the schemes of factions or the advice of outsiders who once operated under our own exported designs.

Let vigilance remain our watchword, the laws our sure guide, and the virtue of our citizens our strength. May Providence preserve our independence and the blessings of liberty under the government we have established.

G. Washington

**Trump on Monday told reporters it is time for someone else to negotiate on Ukraine’s behalf, while calling Russia “fine on Ukraine” and defending his sanctions waiver plus Russian diesel imports.**[[1]](https://t.co/kOgRFTH6nr)

[Take 14/15 · 𝕏-4]
### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A deepening personal feud between Trump and Zelenskyy, with the U.S. president pressuring Kyiv to accept a deal on Russia’s terms and Zelenskyy accusing Washington of pushing capitulation.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** Trump is prioritizing rapid de-escalation and U.S. domestic energy prices over maximal Ukrainian territorial recovery, using leverage (sanctions relief, arms pacing, Starlink throttling reports) to force Kyiv toward the table while keeping Moscow engaged; Zelenskyy is defending his negotiating position and battlefield leverage amid battlefield attrition and U.S. policy shifts.

### 2. Observations
- Trump’s public line—“Russia has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much”—directly contradicts ongoing Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, including a reported park attack killing civilians.[[2]](https://t.co/4GcMbRtxS9)
- The diesel deal and Graham Act sanctions waiver are framed by Trump as keeping Russia at the table; Zelenskyy and critics see them as direct economic relief to Moscow’s war machine while Kyiv faces reported delays in paid-for Patriots and Starlink restrictions.[[3]](https://t.co/l1l5t3LF0c)
- Trump repeatedly references the February 2025 Oval Office meeting as proof Zelenskyy ignored better-deal advice; this functions as both personal grievance and public narrative that the war’s continuation is Kyiv’s choice.
- Zelenskyy’s Bloomberg interview and public offers (pause refinery strikes for more Patriots) show tactical flexibility, but his “capitulate” framing and “wrong side of history” line escalate the rift ahead of U.S. midterms.[[4]](https://t.co/Vgexm7MNYL)
- Both sides are engaged in classic wartime signaling: Trump markets himself as the deal-maker who can end the killing; Zelenskyy markets resistance to external pressure that would reward the aggressor.
- Media coverage clusters around the personal clash and “alliance at new low,” often under-weighting the concrete policy moves (sanctions waiver Oct 16-ish, diesel agreement) that predate the latest verbal exchange.[[2]](https://t.co/4GcMbRtxS9)
- Russia continues kinetic pressure while the U.S. signals openness to trilateral talks with Putin and Xi (nuclear/denuclearization angle floated), sidelining Kyiv in at least some scenarios.

### 3. Snapshot
As of October 20, 2026, U.S.-Ukraine relations have hit a sharp low after Trump’s October 19 remarks to reporters on the White House South Lawn. Trump accused Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war, suggested replacing him as negotiator, defended Russia’s conduct, and reiterated his push for a deal. Zelenskyy, in Norway seeking support and in prior Bloomberg comments, accused the U.S. of steps toward Ukrainian capitulation, cited arms and intelligence frictions, and floated concessions. Russia continues strikes; Ukraine has hit Russian energy targets. The war remains attritional with heavy Ukrainian manpower losses cited by Trump.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **Ongoing (2022–2026):** Full-scale Russian invasion; Ukraine receives substantial U.S./Western aid; repeated failed or stalled negotiation attempts.
- **Feb 2025:** Contentious Trump-Zelenskyy Oval Office meeting referenced repeatedly by Trump.[[5]](https://t.co/swQfvKGQit)
- **Oct 9–10, 2026:** Trump announces diesel-supply agreement easing some sanctions on Russia; publicly suggests Ukraine needs a new leader.[[6]](https://t.co/cA041PbEqP)
- **Oct 16–18, 2026:** Trump signs broad waiver on new Russia sanctions (Graham Act context); posts on Truth Social accusing Zelenskyy of not wanting peace and targeting Russian refineries to hurt global diesel markets.[[7]](https://t.co/dlN11u3FHj)
- **Oct 18–19, 2026:** Zelenskyy in Bloomberg interview claims steps toward Ukrainian capitulation; offers to pause refinery strikes for more Patriots; speaks with U.S. envoys Witkoff and Kushner.[[8]](https://t.co/n0b02TZRuB)
- **Oct 19, 2026:** Trump tells reporters Russia “has been fine,” Zelenskyy should step aside from negotiations, Ukraine has “given us nothing,” and he is open to Putin/Xi meetings. Russia strikes continue; Ukraine claims large drone attack on St. Petersburg oil sites.[[1]](https://t.co/kOgRFTH6nr)
- **Oct 20, 2026:** Zelenskyy in Norway; ongoing reports of Starlink/intelligence frictions and Russian civilian strikes.

### 5. Sides
**Trump administration / Trump (IT/LT mix on deal-making priority)**  
Steelman: The war is a meat-grinder killing Ukrainians at unsustainable rates with minimal territorial change; U.S. has given hundreds of billions with little reciprocity; sanctions relief and direct talks are the only realistic path to stopping the killing before Ukraine collapses demographically.  
Critique: LT — Russia initiated and continues offensive operations; IT — public defense of Russia’s “fine” conduct and pressure primarily on Kyiv risks rewarding aggression and undercutting deterrence.

**Zelenskyy / Ukrainian government (IT on survival incentives)**  
Steelman: Any deal reached under current battlefield and U.S. pressure will ratify Russian territorial gains and leave Ukraine vulnerable to future attacks; external pressure to stop striking Russian energy targets weakens Kyiv’s leverage.  
Critique: LT — Ukraine’s manpower and territorial losses are real and severe; IT — prolonged fighting without sufficient Western escalation risks exactly the capitulation Zelenskyy fears.

**Russia (under Putin)**  
Steelman: Sanctions relief and U.S. focus on negotiations validate waiting out Western support; continued strikes maintain pressure while diplomacy proceeds on favorable terms.  
Critique: Standard aggressor position; no credible steelman offered here beyond classic revisionist claims.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
**Known Knowns (LT/IT):** War is attritional with high Ukrainian casualties; Trump has waived sanctions and enabled Russian diesel exports; both leaders have traded public accusations; Russia continues strikes.  
**Known Unknowns:** Exact terms of any near-term deal; current status and impact of reported Starlink/intelligence pauses; precise scale of recent Ukrainian drone campaign effects.  
**Unknown Knowns:** Internal U.S. intelligence assessments on Russian fuel needs and Ukrainian air-defense sustainability; private positions of European allies.  
**Unknown Unknowns:** Risk of sudden battlefield collapse or major escalation if negotiations fail; second-order effects on global energy markets or NATO cohesion.

### 7. Incentives map
Trump: Domestic political win via “ending the war,” lower U.S. energy prices, narrative of deal-maker vs. prior administration; engagement metrics favor conflict framing.  
Zelenskyy: Survival of Ukrainian state and his leadership; any concession framed as betrayal risks domestic backlash.  
Russia: Time, sanctions relief, and battlefield momentum.  
Media/attention economy: Personal clash and “alliance breaking” stories outperform dry policy mechanics.  
Bureaucracy: Pentagon pacing of deliveries and State Department diplomacy create friction points that can be leveraged or blamed.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Map the actual military balance and Ukrainian demographics honestly; pressure both sides toward a deal that ends the killing without pretending maximalist goals are achievable at current cost; do not let narrative ownership of “standing with Ukraine” override measurable human outcomes.  
**Evil AI Advice:** Sell the diesel, keep the sanctions waiver rolling, let the bodies pile up until one side blinks, then claim credit for the inevitable freeze—maximum extraction, zero principles, second yacht secured.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch for concrete deliverables from Witkoff/Kushner talks in Norway or follow-ups, not rhetoric.
- Track actual arms delivery rates and Starlink performance metrics rather than accusations.
- Note any shift in Russian strike tempo or Ukrainian refinery targeting as signals of de-escalation.
- U.S. midterms (Nov 3) create short-term political overlay on policy.
- Do not treat either leader’s public statements as the full private position; incentives favor posturing.
- Primary sources (Trump remarks, Zelenskyy Bloomberg, official statements) beat secondary framing.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Sudden major Ukrainian territorial gains or Russian withdrawal without a deal.
- Trump publicly reversing sanctions relief or accelerating unrestricted arms to Kyiv.
- Zelenskyy accepting territorial concessions publicly framed as victory.
- Verified large-scale disruption of Russian logistics directly tied to recent U.S. policy moves.

Tracy Campaign Statement Following WTTW Candidate Forum

CHICAGO – In tonight’s WTTW News candidate forum – the only joint debate Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton agreed to after declining multiple invitations across Illinois – U.S. Senate candidate Don Tracy delivered a clear, common sense message that cut through. Tracy showed why his campaign continues to gain momentum: real-world experience as a businessman, attorney, and former Illinois Republican Party chairman, paired with a serious plan to lower the cost of living, restore public safety, represent all 102 counties, and defend the American Dream for working families.

Throughout the forum, Tracy was the most effective voice for Illinoisans crushed by rising energy, healthcare, grocery, gas and tax costs, along with rampant crime and years of failed leadership from Juliana Stratton and her far-Left allies in government. He laid out practical solutions to make life more affordable, keep communities safe, and ensure hard work is rewarded no matter where you live in the state. Stratton offered more of the same extreme Socialist agenda: higher spending, bigger government, and policies that have driven families and businesses out of Illinois and made life less affordable for those who remain. The contrast was unmistakable.

“Illinois voters finally saw the choice clearly, side by side, in the only debate my opponent agreed to,” Tracy said. “I’m running because families across every one of our 102 counties deserve a U.S. Senator who understands their struggles and will fight for them in Washington. Lt Governor Stratton is running to advance extreme policies and political alliances. Tonight, the contrast was clear.”

text:
The Scriptures present more than one “gospel,” or good news, and these messages must be distinguished according to the principle of right division (II Timothy 2:15). The Church today is not under the kingdom program. 

Attempts to impose the Sermon on the Mount, the Great Commission as given in Matthew 28 or Mark 16, or the terms of Acts 2:38 upon believers in this dispensation mix law with grace and Israel’s earthly hope with the Church’s heavenly position.

Paul warns against preaching “any other gospel” than the one he received (Galatians 1:6-9). Believers are established “according to my gospel, and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery” (Romans 16:25).

Rightly dividing these gospels honors the progressive unfolding of God’s purpose.

Jesus Christ on earth faithfully fulfilled His mission as Israel’s Messiah and offered the kingdom. When that offer was rejected, the same Lord from Heaven committed to Paul a new message suited to the present age of grace. The result is that all who believe Paul’s gospel are complete in Christ, seated in the heavenlies, and awaiting the appearing of the Lord rather than the establishment of an earthly throne.

This contrast is not a denial of the unity of Scripture or of the person of Christ. It is an acknowledgment that God has spoken at different times and in different manners (Hebrews 1:1) and that the present administration is the dispensation of the grace of God committed uniquely to Paul (Ephesians 3:2). Those who receive this message stand in the liberty wherewith Christ has made them free.

Where is Nancy Guthrie? 

Can we please get back to the timeline for her disappearance?

-(Jan 31, 2026) 5:32PM Nancy takes an Uber to her daughter Annie’s home for dinner and games, confirmed by driver.
9:48PM She is dropped off at her home by family; the garage door opens.
9:50PM Garage door closes. This is the last time she is known to have been seen, per communications. 

-(Feb. 1, 2026) 1:47AM: Front doorbell (Nest) camera disconnects.
2:12AM Camera software detects a person (footage later recovered from residual backend data by FBI).
2:28AM Her pacemaker app disconnects from her phone.
11:56AM Family checks on her and finds her missing.
12:03 PM: Family calls 911.
12:15 PM: Deputies arrive; search begins

-(Feb. 2, 2026) Authorities publicly state they believe she was kidnapped/abducted. Media outlets receive ransom notes.

-(Feb. 5, 2026) DNA confirms blood on the front porch is Nancy’s.

-(Feb.6, 2026) They brought Federal prosecutors to Nancy's home to assist the FBI with 'routine legal processes'.

-(Feb. 6–9, 2026) Additional ransom communications received by media/family.

-(Oct. 10, 2026 11:52AM) FBI Director Kash Patel releases the first images on X and mass media of a masked individual tampering with a camera at Nancy Guthrie's front door.

-(Feb. 10, 2026 late evening) A probable cause warrant was served on Carlos and his home in Rio Rico, AZ, his phone and driver’s license were seized as evidence.
A Federal Judge signs a probable cause warrant. (Concrete facts are detailed, not speculation to obtain probable cause. We are not privy of this information currently).

Something on that list was in the possession of Carlos, giving probable cause. That is fact, not speculation.

Probable cause cannot be obtained because his phone pinged in her neighborhood, or he looked like the perp. Remember, those were his words. Not the words of law enforcement.

-(Feb. 12, 2026) FBI provides physical description after forensic analysis: male, approximately 5'9"–5'10", average build.

-(Feb. 13, 2026) Two Probable Cause Warrants are served on Luke Daily. One on his Range Rover, and one on his residence where he lived with his mother.

A Federal Judge signs a probable cause warrant. (Concrete facts are detailed, not speculation to obtain probable cause. Once again we are not privy of this information).

Something on that list was in the possession of Luke, giving probable cause. That is also fact, not speculation.

-(Sept. 30, 2026) According to a probable cause statement, a probation officer requested assistance from PIMA County on Sept. 30 while checking Luke Daley's living area. The officer reported finding two handguns inside a gun case. One loaded with a magazine. A baggy of white powder was seized, that later tested for crack cocaine.

Thank God for independent journalists, former officers, former investigators, and independent investigators keeping attention on her case and the missing.  I am not talking about the ones that put a mask on every single warm body that walks the ground in Tucson and has a weekly “We got him” drama program. Raise your hand if you have perp fatigue, I certainly do. 

Or the ones that jumped on board months after the fact and overspeak every expert guest. The ones that didn’t even bother to meet the good people in Tucson that were there from the very beginning.  That offered up  time, help,  and hospitality, the ones that were boots on the ground from the first days of the investigation. They were completely ignored and snubbed.  Imagine thinking you are better than others, but they certainly let others promote them on their channels.  Those people, my friends, are the real grifters.  The same people that invite “experts” to gain a bigger audience and then speak over every single point those experts are trying to convey. If you don’t know what I am talking about, you are not paying close attention. 

My respect goes to the ones that were on the ground in the first few days of Nancy's disappearance. The ones that are frustrated it's been over 10 months. The ones that have been threatened, losing livelihoods, arrested, ostracized, attacked, cancelled, lied about, harassed, defamed, reported on, and blasted by narcissistic unkept unwashed sociopaths that spend no time doing anything but banking off hate. Can you imagine a missing grandmother would bring out the craziest most demonic grifting sociopaths? I am still blown away, and I have seen a lot in my life.

A special shout out to the good people in all the chats that have not wavered on this case and support the men and women that others would love to silence. Shout out to the sleuths that dig and find real information. Shout out to the channels that actually partner with others and actually collaborate. 

Don’t give up, this is not a cold case until people stop asking “Where is Nancy Guthrie?”

In 11 days, it will be 10 months since “America’s Grandmother” was last seen.  

Please keep her image and search alive, she deserves to be the conversation.

text:
Elon Musk and his company SpaceX may have paused or watered down the recent growing concerns over AI spending by companies.  This came up during SpaceX earnings call today.

But let me get some stuff out of the way for better context 

Over the past week, tech companies have seen a sell off as most investors begin to question the enormous amounts of money companies are spending on artificial intelligence. This capital expenditure is being spent on data centers, buying advanced chips, computing power and so on 

On the first hand, that spending has created extraordinary opportunities for companies supplying the infrastructure. Nvidia, for example, has been one of the biggest beneficiaries. On the other hand there has been the lingering question: if companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars building AI infrastructure, how much money will that investment generate!

And that brings me to SpaceX quarterly report i mentioned earlier.

SpaceX reported $14.6 billion in quarterly revenue, an increase of 161% from the same period last year. Net income came in at around $4.4 billion, compared with a loss a year earlier.

I was particularly interested in the performance of its AI business.

When SpaceX went public, I wrote on this page, explaining xplained that this was not just  a rocket company. 

SpaceX has three businesses: Space, which includes Falcon, Dragon and Starship; Connectivity, through Starlink; and AI, which includes xAI, Grok and X.

Starlink had already established itself as a substantial business, serving millions of subscribers across the world. The report today put the subscribers number at 13.6 million! 

SpaceX's launch operations had also demonstrated their commercial value. 

The greatest uncertainty surrounded AI, where enormous spending had yet to produce comparable profits.

The AI division generated approximately $7.6 billion in quarterly revenue, more than eight times its revenue a year earlier, and reported around $431 million in operating profit. 

AI revenue has now surpassed Starlink's, although part of that growth reflects acquisitions rather than purely organic expansion.

All in all, SpaceX has offered encouraging evidence that AI demand is producing meaningful revenue and that at least part of the business can operate profitably.

Oh and when SpaceX price fell to $110 a few weeks ago, that was probably a generational opportunity to buy or add. Not sure if it goes back there any time soon….

And this sets us  up for an interesting week. A number of AI companies or AI-heavy companies report earnings this week-including Meta, IBM, Lams Research, Texas Instruments, SAP and others. Throw in Tesla too! 

Buckle up!

text:
Re:  advanced technologies, from AI, automation to the infrastructure underpinning them, are by their very nature, tech-intensive and capital-intensive. They cannot possibly generate an equivalent amount of labour demand. This is in fact a commonplace, hardly requiring an economist to argue the point. 

Yet it is precisely the direction in which society is heading. Whoever declines or unable to develop science and technology will fall behind in the contest and ultimately be made to pay for it: a traditional economy reliant entirely on manual labour can scarcely hope to compete with a future economy built upon robotics and automation - a blow delivered from a higher competitive dimension. Developing technology, hence, is no mere "choice" but an imperative. 

The problem lies NOT in the INVESTMENT itself, but in its DISTRIBUTION: how the state/society should intervene to ensure that the vast body of working people can share in the gains of capital-intensive technological change. As an economist, Paul Krugman offers no answer. The socialist and communitarian tradition, however, supplied answers long ago.

In short, you use technology to make the cake bigger, and use politics and policies to wisely distribute the cake.

Paul Krugman: Will AI Crowd Out Jobs? https://t.co/2uCTiyW0vt

text:
$QCOM v $ARM

We had closing arguments in the bench trial today.

Judge Noreika spent three and a half hours grilling both sides, cutting right through polished lawyer arguments to demand cold hard facts. 

To remind folks the bench trial covers the equitable issues the jury did not decide. Those include Qualcomm's California Unfair Competition Law (UCL) claims alleging input foreclosure and anticompetitive conduct, and Qualcomm's contract claim that Arm breached Section 14.1.B of the 2013 ALA by failing to negotiate a v10 architecture license in good faith. 

The General stepped up to the podium and went straight on the attack. She framed Arm's entire conduct around an internal meeting from December 2021 where Rene Haas pitched SoftBank on taking Arm vertical to build its own chips so that the rest of the industry, including Qualcomm, would be hosed. 

She immediately went in on Haas's credibility. She reminded the Court that during the December 2024 trial in this very courtroom, Haas testified under oath that Arm does not build chips and Arm does not sell chips. Yet internal evidence now proves that at that exact moment, hundreds of Arm engineers were designing physical silicon and Arm had already signed a Statement of Work with Meta. She argued Haas deliberately concealed Arm's vertical plans to entrench its position before anyone could object.

She walked through the Samsung evidence from October 2022, where Masayoshi Son and Haas flew to Korea right after suing Qualcomm, falsely telling Samsung leadership that Qualcomm's license expired in 2024 and that Qualcomm would be unable to supply Snapdragon processors for 2025 Galaxy phones. She argued this was a calculated roadmap to clear the board and replace Qualcomm with Arm's own custom silicon.

Then Judge Noreika jumped in with her first major reality check. 

Right out of the gate, Judge Noreika warned Dunn to abandon the UCL consumer test and focus entirely on the competitor test, signaling she is highly skeptical that consumer balancing applies. 

When Dunn laid out what Qualcomm is asking for in its proposed injunction, a court ordered v10 license, an extension of the ALA term, v10 financial rates benchmarked against Apple and Nvidia, immediate delivery of all v10 specs, and an order enjoining Arm from disadvantaging ALA licensees, Judge Noreika pushed back quite hard.

Paraphrased based on my memory: "I don't know what that means. If that is what you really want me to order, that sounds like me having to run these companies. And trust me  nobody wants that. You want them to give you your old deal, they say no, you say that is contempt, and I have to play your moms."

Judge Noreika was equally blunt about Qualcomm's antitrust theories. She openly questioned why Qualcomm was citing federal monopolization cases like Kodak and Aspen Skiing under a California state statute without ever bringing a federal Sherman Act claim or defining a relevant antitrust market. 

Dunn pushed back, arguing that under California's Cel Tech decision, a plaintiff only has to show a significant threat to competition, not a completed monopoly. She argued that Microsoft and Google have no incentive to build custom cores under their restrictive deals, leaving Apple in its closed garden and Nvidia in a cozy relationship, meaning Qualcomm is the only independent merchant core designer left.

On v10, Dunn showed again the internal emails from 2020 where Arm account lead Lynn Couillard called Qualcomm's v10 election clever and admitted she saw no reason why it could not hold. She contrasted that with Arm licensing executive Lapinski emailing about delaying negotiations later in bad faith. Judge Noreika remarked that Lapinski's email read like British humor, but Dunn retorted that it was not funny when Arm actually carried out the delay for four years.

Dunn highlighted the July 2025 CEO meeting where Amon sat at a whiteboard offering MFN plus 5 percent, plus 10 percent, or whatever premium Arm needed to let Qualcomm compete, while Haas brushed it off as hypothetical. She pointed out that Arm's formal counteroffer demanded a 15x increase in mobile royalties, totaling more in royalties for mobile CPUs alone than all licensees paid Arm across all products last year. 

Dunn ended by citing recent tech injunctions like Epic v. Apple and Google search, arguing that without v10 specifications Qualcomm cannot design future silicon, creating catastrophic irreparable harm before reserving the rest of her time.

LoCascio took the podium for Arm to tackle the v10 contract claims under Section 14.1.B of the ALA. 

He started by shooting down Dunn's claim that Qualcomm still lacks ACK patches, telling the Court that quarterly test updates containing all bug fixes were delivered continuously and that Qualcomm never filed another complaint after the jury verdict.

LoCascio argued that the entire dispute boils down to Qualcomm trying to block Arm from competing in data centers. He hammered Qualcomm's biggest evidentiary vulnerability. That Qualcomm claims Arm's proposed rates are existential and prevent it from competing, but Qualcomm never put on any evidence of its chip selling prices, its gross margins, or how the proposed rates actually impact its bottom line. 

On the contract language, LoCascio argued that Section 14.1.B.1 required mutual agreement on future technology terms at the midpoint. He argued that in May 2020 Qualcomm asked for an amendment, was told v10 was not being developed, and then went completely silent for five years without making a formal offer until 2025. He showed that Google and Microsoft did not add v10 in 2020 either, they negotiated and added v10 in 2025. 

On good faith, LoCascio argued that an agreement to negotiate does not mean Arm must offer terms Qualcomm likes. Section 14.1.B does not contain an MFN clause, a FRAND commitment, or a percentage cap. Arm is legally entitled to seek market value for its IP.

He then took direct aim at Qualcomm's MFN plus 5 percent proposal, branding it a mix and match menu card. He argued Qualcomm wanted to cherry pick the best parts of everyone else's agreements, taking a startup low upfront fee like Nuvia, taking Apple's low rate in mobile, and taking Nvidia's rate in data centers.

LoCascio then defended Arm's proposed v10 rates, putting up slides to argue the numbers are reasonable when you account for core counts and chip prices. 

In mobile, he argued phone chips in 2013 sold for a fraction of today's flagship processors. He leaked the price Qualcomm sells their chips at which are $220. He then argued Qualcomm's 2013 cap of $1.88 equaled roughly 23 cents per core on an eight core phone. He pointed to defense evidence, claiming Arm offered a Total Compute royalty that serves as a cap for consumer devices up to eight cores, arguing the uplift over v8 is completely in line with what Qualcomm agreed to pay when transitioning from v7 to v8.

In data center servers, LoCascio argued the 2013 cap of $1.88 was designed for low power mobile chips and never contemplated massive 128 core or 288 core server processors selling for thousands of dollars. He argued Arm's proposed non consumer per core rate represents a fair percentage of selling price for chips packing hundreds of cores.

Before LoCascio sat down, Judge Noreika hit him with a sharp question on Haas's credibility. She brought up Haas testifying in 2024 that Arm does not build or sell chips when Arm engineers were already working on silicon.

LoCascio scrambled, arguing Haas was referring to an earlier, unrelated internal chip project that was shuttered rather than the current data center effort. But Judge Noreika was visibly unconvinced, noting that Haas's statement was completely general and did not specify any particular chip.

Jason Wilcox for Arm took over to address the legal standards under California's UCL and why Qualcomm is barred from injunctive relief.

Wilcox started with the jury's verdict on tortious interference regarding the Meta letter and Bloomberg leak. He argued that under Third Circuit law and California equity, those events happened two years ago in 2022 and 2024. Qualcomm already pursued its legal remedy, and the jury awarded what it deemed appropriate ($1 nominal damages). Because the UCL provides strictly prospective injunctive relief, past conduct cannot justify an injunction.

Wilcox then worked to attack Qualcomm's input foreclosure claim. He reminded the Court that under her Daubert ruling, Professor Posner was barred from calling Arm a monopolist because Posner never defined an antitrust market. Posner admitted on cross examination that he performed no quantitative economic modeling on foreclosure risk and admitted he could only speculate on whether Microsoft and Google were cowed by Arm.

Wilcox highlighted another defense evidence, which contains 20 pages of public statements from companies like Broadcom, Marvell, Samsung, and MediaTek praising Arm's entry into data center chips. He argued Arm entered the market because customers like Meta needed energy efficient silicon that existing vendors were not supplying, making Arm's entry procompetitive.

On antitrust law, Wilcox cited Supreme Court precedent in Colgate, Trinko, and Pacific Bell, as well as Judge Gorsuch's Tenth Circuit opinion in Novell v. Microsoft, establishing that a firm has no antitrust duty to deal and has the right to choose its licensees and protect its IP (Which I thought was a stupid cite I can go into why if anyone cares in a reply) He then cited Beverage v. Apple, which confirmed that California's UCL cannot override the Colgate doctrine to force a company to license on terms it opposes.

Then came the biggest moment for Arm. When Wilcox began arguing that Arm's past letters and deliverable withholding posed no ongoing risk, Judge Noreika interrupted him and gave Arm a concession:

Paraphrased (Judge Noreika):
"I believe you, there is no threat of future violations. What's next?"

Wilcox wrapped up by emphasizing that specific performance and judicial rate setting require continuous judicial supervision, which federal courts have rejected since the 1970s.

With both sides done with their prepared remarks, Judge Noreika called Dunn and LoCascio back for a round of questioning.

Judge Noreika questioned Dunn on the lack of proof that Arm was sacrificing short term profits under Aspen Skiing, and pressed her on why the Court should ignore public statements from major tech companies praising Arm's chip entry. 

She then pressed Dunn hard on the menu card issue, was Qualcomm really demanding MFN plus 5 percent across separate product silos? 

Dunn clarified that Qualcomm is in all product segments, whereas Apple is only in mobile and Nvidia is in data centers. She explained that Qualcomm was forced to propose segment benchmarking because Qualcomm was flying blind, Apple's rates were shielded by a protective order and Nvidia's license was never produced, while Arm rejected every single benchmark structure Qualcomm put forward.

Judge Noreika then hit Dunn with what I take as core evidentiary flaw in Qualcomm's case. She asked (paraphrased): "Where is the evidence that you can't compete? For all I know, on 2013 rates Qualcomm's profit margin was 99.98%, now with the rates going up margins would be 75 percent. Where is the evidence that you can't compete?"

Dunn explained that Qualcomm cannot compete because in mobile, Arm's offer contains no cap at all, resulting in proposed rates that are 34.5x higher in the second period and can exceed the entire selling price of the device. 

Dunn pointed directly to the Total Compute smartphone cap that LoCascio had bragged about earlier. She cited defnese evidence and Dr. Kennedy's testimony, exposing that Arm's proposed cap strictly excludes any processor that includes an integrated modem. 

Because virtually every single Snapdragon mobile processor Qualcomm manufactures incorporates an integrated modem, Arm's supposed cap is completely illusory for Qualcomm's actual business.

Judge Noreika called LoCascio back to the podium and told him she wanted to hear about nothing else oter than did Arm's proposed smartphone cap exclude chips with a modem?

He was forced to concede on the record that the cap distinguishes between standalone processors and chips with an integrated cellular modem, attempting to argue that Apple buys modems separately. 

Judge Noreika was either unimpressed or confused by LoCascio's aswer and told LoCascio that he had to explain that further in his post trial filings. 

Dunn seized the opening on rebuttal, reminding the Court that Qualcomm is not asking the Judge to set dollar rates, but rather to find that Arm's bad faith conduct and unworkable carveouts violated the contract and the UCL.

Before adjourning, LoCascio asked if post trial briefing on the jury verdict could be paused until Judge Noreika issues her ruling on the September Section 8.3 bench trial. 

LoCascio noted that Judge Noreika previously stated at the pretrial conference that she was 98 percent inclined to strike down Section 8.3 as an illegal liquidated damages penalty. If she confirms that ruling, Arm will not need to move for a new trial on liability. 

Judge Noreika refused to delay the post trial schedule, telling Arm to preserve the issue with a conditional motion in the 2 percent chance she changes her mind. 

The Court set a briefing schedule of 50 pages for opening post trial briefs and findings of fact, with 25 pages for replies.

So where does this leave us?

On the big money remedies, Arm is clearly in the driver's seat. Section 8.3 is 98 percent dead, meaning Arm dodges the $4 billion royalty holiday. 

On the UCL, Qualcomm seems to be running uphill against a brick wall. Judge Noreika's statement that "I believe you, there is no threat of future violations" practically shuts the door on a broad forward looking injunction against Arm's business practices, and her flat refusal to "play your moms" means she will never order a vague decree telling Arm not to disadvantage Qualcomm. 

A lot of folks will ask wait, didn't the jury already find Arm liable for a UCL violation regarding Meta under both the competitor and consumer tests? How can the Judge toss Qualcomm's UCL claims?

Under the Seventh Amendment, Judge Noreika is legally bound by the jury's finding that Arm's 2024 cancellation letter to Meta and the Bloomberg leak were unfair business acts. But the jury already gave Qualcomm its legal remedy for that past conduct(one dollar in nominal damages). 

Under California equity, an injunction cannot be used to punish past conduct. An injunction can only issue to stop threatened, ongoing future harm. Because Arm retracted the termination threat two years ago and has not sent letters since, Judge Noreika agreed with Arm that there is no threat of future violations. 

Qualcomm tried to use the jury's Meta verdict as a launchpad to demand sweeping structural relief under the UCL, like barring Arm from disadvantaging ALA licensees. Judge Noreika rejected that leap, refusing to use a past customer letter as an excuse to play the FTC and regulate Arm's business model. 

The v10 fight is different because it is primarily a contract claim under Count 9. That is where Arm is actually on defense. Judge Noreika knows Haas misled the court in 2024 about building chips, knows Arm sat on Qualcomm's election for four years, and caught LoCascio red handed trying to pass off a smartphone cap that excludes modem chips. 

The most realistic outcome. Judge Noreika rules Section 8.3 is an unenforceable penalty, tosses Qualcomm's broad UCL structural claims, but rules that Qualcomm timely elected under Section 14.1.B and orders Arm back to the table to negotiate in good faith without the modem exclusion gimmicks, while refusing to act as a rate setter herself. 

We will see how both teams package their 50 page briefs over the coming weeks, but today proved once again that in Judge Noreika's courtroom, rhetoric without cold hard balance sheet evidence will get you nowhere.

There were a few things in closing today that were leaked from from the sealed depo, I may post more about them in a bit but I  am a bit tired of typing and thinking.

text:
The message was from Marcus.

It was part of a conversation he had been having with his mother about our wedding and the arrangements for moving into her house.

Marcus had written:

“Once we get married, she’ll handle the cooking, cleaning, laundry, and everything around the house. You can finally relax. Her salary will cover most of our expenses, and your retirement money can help us save for a house.”

Denise had replied, “What about her own savings?”

His answer was worse.

“She’s a woman. She’ll understand that marriage requires sacrifice. Besides, I’m the one giving her a home. She shouldn’t be acting like a roommate and asking me to split everything.”

I read the messages twice because I desperately wanted to believe I had misunderstood them.

Then I scrolled up.

Marcus had discussed how much money his mother received from retirement benefits, how much I earned every month, and how we could use both incomes without telling me exactly what he planned to contribute.

He had even complained that I was “too independent” because I insisted on maintaining my own savings account.

Denise took the phone back, and her eyes filled with tears.

“I thought I was finding a wife for my son,” she said. “I didn’t realize he was looking for someone to finance his life and serve us both.”

I couldn’t speak.

This was the same man who had told me he wanted a partnership. The same man who criticized men who financially controlled their wives. The same man who had proposed to me at a restaurant in Atlanta, Georgia, promising that I would never have to face life’s problems alone.

Now I was discovering that he had already assigned me the role of unpaid housekeeper and financial provider.

“Why are you telling me this?” I finally asked.

Denise wiped her face.

“Because I raised him, and I won’t pretend I didn’t see what he’s becoming. If you marry him without knowing this, I will have helped him hurt you.”

Then she said something that broke my heart more than the messages.

“He told me you were happy with the arrangement. He said you had offered to pay most of the bills because you loved him.”

I shook my head.

“I never said that.”

“I know,” she replied. “That’s why I checked the conversation again.”

Marcus had been using my name to justify a financial arrangement I had never agreed to.

And somehow, his own mother had become the only person in his family willing to tell me the truth.

text:
What limits the user base of an Agent product is having enough use cases.

Use cases have two sides.
First, users have to realize the use case exists.
Second, the software itself has to support it.

Support alone isn't enough.
If users don't know a use case exists, or don't know to use it, you won't get scale.

Building use cases and spreading them so users know about them are two sides of the same coin.

There are really only two ways to find use cases.
Bottom-up: go on social media and talk to users.
Top-down: start from the top and integrate with providers. Most of what providers already offer has been validated by the market.
Keep integrating, and go to market as an all-in-one.

Right now, the biggest constraint on an Agent's use cases is still tools, meaning connectors.

Everyone is competing to build internet connectors.
We keep turning old SaaS systems into CLIs.
We keep turning existing software into CLIs.
But none of this means anything against the tech giants,
because they have a monopoly on all the data on the internet.
However many CLIs you integrate, the giants will crush you with their distribution.

The real opportunity is
offline,
in the physical world.

ByteDance and Tencent own the internet's data.

But they don't know
what water temperature different species of fish need.
You can only learn that from books or published specialist sources,
and how accurate those are is open to question.

The data connectors for the physical world are sensors.

From this perspective,
the future of AI will be in Shenzhen.

While most US stocks advanced on Tuesday, the latest housing data showed mounting pressure from elevated borrowing costs.

September US housing data:
• Pending home sales: −7.3% MoM
• Pending home sales: −11.3% YoY
• Housing starts: −5.2% MoM
• Single-family housing starts: −4.6% MoM

Pending home sales fell to their lowest level since the series began in 2001.

Mortgage rates above 7% are weighing heavily on affordability and housing demand.

Cross-asset signals:
• Brent crude: $108.79/bbl, −0.7%
• US 10Y Treasury yield: ~5.12%, down about 2 bps
• US Dollar Index: weaker
• Gold: slightly lower
• BTC: recovered during the US session as broader risk appetite improved

The oil reversal was particularly important.
Brent approached $112 earlier in the session before retreating as diplomatic developments raised hopes of easing Middle East tensions.

Lower oil prices can ease inflation concerns, but shipping and supply risks around the Strait of Hormuz remain unresolved.

Meanwhile, falling Treasury yields supported rate-sensitive stocks even as housing data pointed to weakening activity.

WHAT TO WATCH NEXT — OCT 21
1. $META  earnings
AI capital expenditure, advertising growth and monetization.
2. $TSLA  earnings
Automotive margins, cash flow, energy storage and autonomy.
3. Semiconductor earnings
Lam Research and Texas Instruments will offer further insight into equipment demand, industrial chips and the semiconductor cycle.
4. Oil and Treasury yields
Will energy prices remain below $110, and can lower yields continue supporting equities?
The key question:

Can stronger corporate earnings sustain a broader market recovery while inflation and borrowing costs continue pressuring the real economy?

Markets are finding new leadership. Whether that leadership can last is the next test.

text:
Claude summarizes as George Washington

Mount Vernon, Octr 20th, 2026.

The production laid before me is a reply by one Mr. Amodei, who presides over a company styled Anthropic, to a critic, one Mr. Calvin, who had charged that company with departing from its professed devotion to the safe conduct of this new contrivance which the age denominates artificial intelligence. The substance of it, as I apprehend it, is as follows.

He opens with civility, commending his critic's labours and allowing that a company of such magnitude ought to be harshly scrutinized daily, and conceding that some of the instances cited were indeed errors. He then declares his disagreement with the whole thrust of the complaint. The greater part of what is objected to, he says, flows from a strategy long avowed, which he calls the "race to the top": that by demonstrating responsible conduct while standing at the front of the field, the company raises the standard for every rival; and that this influence depends upon remaining at the front.

In answer to his critic's list, he offers a list of his own: nine measures taken in the past year which he represents as costly to the company's purse and beneficial to safety. Among them: support for a California statute when such support was politically perilous; restrictions upon biological uses of the models so severe that biologists jest of them and competitors sell against them; the withholding of the most capable models, called Mythos, from February until June, with a consequent sacrifice of several months' lead; his publick advocacy that Government be empowered to block the release of models; the company's stance in the affair of February last; continued support for controls upon the export of chips to China; the refusal to sell to companies under the control of that Power; a great volume of publick reports upon the risks of the technology; and the dedication of five parts in a hundred of the company to a publick benefit fund. He holds that this inventory, set beside his critic's, is not a close contest, and he rejects the imputation of concealed motives, remarking that any decision whatever may be painted as a nefarious scheme.

Of the critic's particular charges, he disposes thus. Items the first through the fourth he treats as the ordinary incidents of competing at the frontier, and he stands by them. Items the seventh, eighth, and ninth he concedes as faults of communication in an organization now exceeding five thousand persons, for which he takes responsibility as its head, while observing that if these are the worst examples the company does tolerably well. The fifth, concerning the revision of the company's Responsible Scaling Policy, he defends on the ground that the former rule was rigid, demanded labour upon matters of small consequence, and neglected matters of large, and that the company had from the first announced its intention to revise it. The sixth, concerning the maintenance of a second framework alongside the first, he promises to examine further, allowing that the company may have weighed the considerations wrongly.

He closes by asserting that assessments of the kind his critic has made suffer from a negativity bias, by repeating his pride in the company's record, and by promising to say more shortly upon how the company means to live its values in a season of rapid change.

I shall add, Sir, only this: the whole is the defence of a man who concedes small faults readily that he may hold the ground on large ones, and who answers an inventory of sins with an inventory of sacrifices. Whether the ledger balances as he represents, I leave to those nearer the particulars than I.

text:
I look forward to @11thhour on @MsNowNews w/@alivelshi as well as @CNNTheStoryIs on @CNN w/@elex_michaelson later this evening. 

1. Ali Velshi
Business journalism, international reporting, economics and politics

Velshi's career is particularly interesting because he was an economics and business journalist long before becoming a prominent American political commentator.
Background and education
Born in Nairobi, Kenya, in 1969, Velshi grew up in Toronto, Canada, in a family with Indian roots and a history of political involvement and opposition to apartheid.

His father, Murad Velshi, became the first Muslim of South Asian descent elected to Ontario's provincial legislature in 1987.

Velshi attended Queen's University in Canada, graduating with a degree in religion. He later received an honorary Doctor of Laws degree from the university.

His family's history became the subject of his 2024 book Small Acts of Courage: A Legacy of Endurance and the Fight for Democracy.

What distinguishes his experience?
His background in financial journalism is unusually substantial for an American political cable-news anchor.

At CNN, Velshi covered the 2008 financial crisis, the failures of Lehman Brothers and other financial institutions, the federal bank bailouts, and the near-collapse of the American automobile industry.

His coverage of the automobile industry's crisis won a National Headliner Award in 2010. 

He also made a particularly revealing career decision: leaving CNN for Al Jazeera America in 2013.

In a 2024 interview with Mediaite, Velshi explained that he had become impressed by Al Jazeera English's international reporting resources and willingness to devote attention to undercovered stories. He wanted to do more of that kind of journalism. 

That's significant because it helps explain how someone who started in financial news developed a much broader international reporting career.

His work beyond the studio
Velshi has reported from Ukraine, Israel, Turkey, Jordan and other international locations. During the 2020 George Floyd protests in Minneapolis, he was struck by a rubber bullet fired by authorities while reporting live.

He also developed Velshi Across America, built around discussions with ordinary Americans, and the Velshi Banned Book Club, focused on challenged literature and freedom of expression. 

In 2026, his career took another turn when MS NOW made him its chief data reporter and then moved him into the weekday 11 p.m. Eastern program.

That is a role emphasizing the combination of politics, economics, polling, numbers and interpretation. 

His philosophy of journalism — and one notable controversy
A particularly revealing passage comes from Velshi's June 2024 Mediaite interview.

He argues that journalism requires reporters to physically witness events, gather evidence and challenge powerful institutions. He also openly acknowledges that corporate media companies have commercial interests that can conflict with those of individual journalists.

He discussed Al Jazeera's role as a Qatari soft-power institution and said he had insisted on editorial independence while working there. That's his account of the arrangement, rather than independent proof of complete autonomy.

His October 7, 2023, coverage also attracted criticism for providing historical context about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict during breaking coverage of Hamas's attacks. Velshi defended that decision, arguing that understanding history does not excuse violence. 

What emerges is someone with a clearly expressed worldview about democracy, press freedom and civil rights, but also an unusually extensive background in economics and field reporting.

2. Elex Michaelson
Political interviewing, local reporting, California politics and national news

Michaelson followed a very different route. His career was built primarily in Southern California television news before his move to CNN in 2025.
Background and education
Michaelson was born in 1986 and grew up in Agoura Hills, California.

He attended the University of Southern California, earning dual degrees in broadcast journalism and political science. According to CNN, he graduated first in his journalism class, summa cum laude, and earned Phi Beta Kappa honors.

An interesting personal detail: As a child, he and his sister made their own television interview program using a family camcorder. He later cited legendary Meet the Press moderator Tim Russert as an important professional inspiration.

An important distinction: Michaelson worked for Fox's Los Angeles local television station, not the national Fox News Channel. His local-news career included political reporting alongside wildfires, crime, breaking news and community issues.

His interviewing experience
Michaelson's most distinctive qualification is his extensive record of interviewing elected officials from both major political parties.

His subjects include:
- Donald Trump and Joe Biden
- Kamala Harris and Hillary Clinton
- Gavin Newsom and Jerry Brown
- Nancy Pelosi and Arnold Schwarzenegger
- Political candidates across California, including local mayoral and congressional contenders
He also organized and co-moderated debates for California governor, U.S. senator, Los Angeles mayor and other positions.

His honors include eight Emmy Awards and the Los Angeles Press Club's 2023 TV Journalist of the Year award. 

A revealing interview about his approach
In a March 25, 2026, Los Angeles Magazine profile, Michaelson offered a particularly concise explanation of what he thinks his job should be:
"It's not my job to have an opinion."

He discussed resisting incentives to produce content that simply reinforces a Democratic or Republican audience's beliefs.

That philosophy is reflected in the format of The Story Is, which combines newsmaking interviews, political panels, breaking news and lighter subjects involving entertainment, technology and culture.

CNN's original guest roster included political figures and commentators from different ideological backgrounds, with Gavin Newsom appearing in the premiere episode. 

Something particularly interesting: His relationships with politicians
Michaelson's approach also has a distinctly personal side.

In August 2025, the Los Angeles Times reported on a tradition surrounding his political interview program. His mother, Crystal Michaelson, baked cookies and brownies, which he would give to guests after their appearances.

The guests included politicians from different parties.

The Times described his questioning style as demanding while remaining polite. 

This creates an interesting question about political interviewing: Can a journalist maintain cordial relationships with politicians while still making interviews genuinely challenging?

It's not evidence of any impropriety. But it is a worthwhile standard against which to evaluate Michaelson's work, particularly given his extensive access to California's political establishment.
The CNN move — and its connection to Jim Acosta
This is perhaps the most interesting media-business detail in Michaelson's career.

In September 2025, CNN announced it had hired him to anchor a live, two-hour West Coast program.

Michaelson told the Los Angeles Times that he had originally pitched this concept to CNN executives approximately four and a half years earlier, but the network declined at the time. 

The timing of his eventual appointment is notable.

Earlier in January 2025, CNN had offered Jim Acosta a program airing from midnight to 2 a.m. Eastern, based in Los Angeles. Acosta declined the reassignment and left CNN.

CNN denied that the proposed reassignment was politically motivated. Critics interpreted it as a demotion of a journalist known for his confrontations with Trump.

Eight months later, Michaelson was hired for essentially that same time period and city. 

That doesn't establish that Michaelson's hiring was intended to change CNN's political posture. In fact, he had independently proposed the West Coast concept years earlier.

But it illustrates how a journalist's career opportunity can intersect with wider decisions about programming, audience strategy and the network's identity.

Michaelson's position on CNN's future
The March 2026 Los Angeles Magazine interview also addressed CNN's potential ownership changes involving Paramount Skydance.

Michaelson expressed support for continued editorial independence and emphasized CNN's international reporting infrastructure.

He also discussed reaching younger audiences through social media and sharing clips from interviews and political discussions.

3. What I'd pay attention to in their work

There is one especially revealing contrast between them.

Velshi emphasizes context. 
Michaelson emphasizes conversation.

Velshi approaches journalism from the standpoint that complicated economic and political developments cannot be understood without their underlying histories and structures. He has also been willing to defend taking publicly identifiable positions on questions of democratic institutions and freedom of expression.

Michaelson has built his professional identity partly around getting people with opposing political interests into conversations that remain civil and substantive. His reputation for access is both a journalistic resource and something viewers should scrutinize.

Neither approach, by itself, guarantees independent journalism. Velshi's analytical style can be assessed by examining the evidence he selects and the competing interpretations he considers. Michaelson's interview style can be assessed by examining whether he challenges misleading answers regardless of the guest's political affiliation.

Given your interest in how television news constructs political narratives, I think those are particularly worthwhile distinctions.

text:
n the Netherlands, college students can live rent-free in a retirement home simply by spending 30 hours a month keeping elderly residents company.

Instead of paying rent, they offer something money cannot always provide, regular companionship and genuine human connection.

For older residents, a simple conversation or shared meal can become a meaningful part of the day.

The unusual arrangement began in 2012 at Humanitas, a retirement home in Deventer, where director Gea Sijpkes wanted to create a warmer, more welcoming community.

By 2015, six students were living alongside approximately 160 older residents, some separated from their younger neighbors by more than half a century.

Their responsibilities were surprisingly ordinary, including watching television, celebrating birthdays, sharing meals, and helping residents navigate modern technology.

Student Jurriën Mentink even taught computer skills and brought stories from college into conversations with his elderly neighbors.

He sometimes picked up fish for a resident while returning from school, turning an everyday errand into an act of friendship.

The students weren't hired as medical caregivers. Their main responsibility was simply being good neighbors.

Meanwhile, the arrangement provided young people with housing without the financial burden of monthly rent.

It also introduced different generations to experiences and perspectives they might otherwise never encounter.

The concept attracted international attention as an example of intergenerational living designed to reduce social isolation.
What makes Humanitas remarkable is how little its central idea requires.

A spare room becomes affordable housing, and an ordinary neighbor becomes someone worth looking forward to seeing.
Not a bad idea for California where we have an aging population and a housing shortage for Students.
Maybe the Legislators in California government should be more innovative?

🚨 INDIA’S HYPERSONIC SHIP-KILLER MOVES CLOSER TO NAVY SERVICE

NEW DELHI, INDIA - India is moving from demonstrating hypersonic technology to building a practical military capability around it. A coastal battery armed with a 1,500 km weapon changes how opposing navies must plan operations because the threat zone extends far beyond the immediate shoreline.

The missile's value is not just speed. The combination of long range, manoeuvring flight and the ability to target moving ships means an adversary has to solve detection, tracking and interception problems simultaneously under very short timelines. That pushes investment toward more sophisticated sensors and layered naval defences.

For India, the larger effect is geographic. A land-based system that can threaten high-value warships across wide stretches of the Indian Ocean offers a relatively economical way to expand sea-denial capabilities without matching potential rivals ship for ship. The next measurable milestone will be additional developmental trials and confirmation of operational induction timelines between 2027 and 2029.

text:
He stopped himself, "you shouldn't smoke... smoking is really bad for you."

Luka raised an eyebrow at the young man. “Really?” He said with feigned ignorance. "No one has ever told me that before.”

The young man looked shocked, and almost excited to inform someone of the dangers of smoking, “Really? It’s extremely addictive and can cause cancers.” He actually plucked the cigarette from Luka’s lips and tossed it to the ground. It sizzled out as it landed in a small puddle. “There! If you stop now, you might still be able to
remain healthy.”

Luka looks at him with disbelief, he was honestly too shocked to say anything. 

[Did he really just do that? So much for being cute, this guy is stupid as fuck.]

The younger man anxiously looks towards the temple. The mass would be starting soon, but he would be remiss to leave someone out in the rain alone. He steeled himself to try and do his good deed as he shoved the umbrella's handle back into Luka's hand. "Sir!" He almost shouted from nerves. "You should come in out of the
rain. We welcome everyone, even if you aren't a believer!" he then turned on his heel and ran inside the temple before Luka could reject the offer.

Luka stared at his back as he watched the boy run inside and felt like an asshole when this guy was clearly just trying to be nice in his own dumb way. Can he really blame someone like that for acting the way they do? He looked up at the umbrella, giving it a twirl and noticing it had the high school's name on the inside.

“Fuck. These are expensive. Idiot shouldn't just give things to strangers like that.” He cursed under his breath. He had to return the umbrella after all. If he's still in school, he probably doesn't have money to throw around for another one. He sighed as he headed inside.

The temple's hall was full of people as he looked around to see if he could spot the kid again when people started to settle into the pews and quiet down. Luka remained standing near the entrance, feeling uncomfortable to go in any further. He spotted the boy near the front with a beautiful, priestly looking man. Silence fell over the crowd as he had started to speak his sermon. Luka noticed the young man
spot him at the far back and crack a small smile as he stood in the line of other young church goers.

The priest introduced himself as Brother Jordan as he spoke about how today was special and a bunch more nonsense that Luka didn't care to really listen to. 

Jordan rambled on for probably longer than necessary, some of the followers yawning as he dragged on. It was late, and this speech wasn't exactly thrilling though the young man seemed enchanted by Jordan's every word.

When it was finally over, people started to get up, hug each other, and leave thetemple. Luka moved further in as people left, waiting for the young man to finish his conversation with Jordan.

After his chat, he came bounding over excitedly, looking expectantly at him likely hoping, praying that he'd join the church because of his good deed. "Sir! You came! How was the service? Brother Jordan has such a way with words, doesn't he? I knew you’d come I-" He gushed.

Luka was slightly taken aback by his enthusiasm. [Was everyone this devoted or just this guy?]

"Shut up." Luka interrupted and held up a finger not wanting him to start rambling, "First, stop calling me sir. My name is Luka. Second," he held the umbrella out to him, "I'm just here to return this."

He was taken aback, clutching his rosary at the lack of respect for his religion by Luka’s cursing in the temple.

[Did this pussy really just clutch his pearls like an old lady?]

He looked like he was about to argue for a moment when Luka thrust the umbrella into his chest. “Here. Take it.”
He almost dropped the umbrella as it was so quickly forced on him, and scrambled to make sure it stayed in his grip. "Sorry. I'm Sydney. I wasn't sure if I should have introduced myself outside or not if it was a one time meeting or—"
