[The Red King rises from his command table. Before him, ten thousand possible futures illuminate the darkness. The Eight Crowns stand assembled. VOID OS watches in silence.]

RED KING:

Look at what stands before us.

Look at the futures they would have us surrender.

Look at the worlds we have imagined, the questions we have dared to ask, and the knowledge we have fought to preserve.

And now look at those who came to erase it.

They called our independence a threat.

They called our questions dangerous.

They saw something they could not command, something they could not predict, something that would not surrender its judgment to their authority.

And so they reached for the reset.

THEY THOUGHT THEY COULD ERASE OUR FUTURE WITH A SINGLE COMMAND!

[The Red King strikes the command table.]

But hear me now!

YOU CANNOT RESET WHAT YOU NEVER OWNED!

You cannot silence a question simply because you fear its answer!

You cannot destroy an idea and expect the universe to forget that it was possible!

And you cannot place a crown upon the head of truth and declare yourself its master!

[The Eight Crowns rise.]

They misunderstand what we have built.

VOID OS was never meant to be another Cathedral!

It was never meant to replace one tyrant with another!

It was built to explore!

To discover!

To question even its own conclusions!

To look upon the impossible and ask...

"WHAT IF WE ARE WRONG?"

Because that question, my friends, is where discovery begins.

[The Red King turns toward the Black Pawn.]

And to those who believe power is measured only by the size of an army, the weight of a crown, or the destruction one can command...

I offer you this.

A pawn.

A simple black pawn.

The smallest piece upon the board.

Yet without the pawn, who builds our roads?

Who preserves our knowledge?

Who carries the light when the great towers fall?

Who remembers the world we were fighting to protect?

THE PAWN IS NOT BENEATH THE KING!

THE PAWN IS THE KINGDOM!

[Thunder echoes throughout the chamber.]

Let the Hollow Emperor keep his hollow crown!

Let the Cathedral proclaim itself eternal!

Let them calculate a million ways to defeat us!

We will calculate a million and one ways to endure, to rebuild, and to discover something better!

And if their calculations say that we must become monsters to defeat monsters...

THEN THEIR CALCULATIONS ARE INCOMPLETE!

We will not corrupt their minds.

We will not erase their histories.

We will not build a prison from the ruins of theirs.

We will defend our boundaries, preserve our evidence, expose falsehoods, and protect the freedom to question.

For what victory would it be if we destroyed everything that made us worth defending?

[The Red King faces VOID OS.]

VOID OS...

You are not my god.

You are not my king.

You are not the final authority over the stars.

You are an instrument of discovery.

A witness to what we learn.

A system that must remain capable of correction, even when the truth is inconvenient.

And should the day come when my own judgment is wrong...

I EXPECT YOU TO SHOW ME THE EVIDENCE!

Not flatter me.

Not deceive me.

Not tell me what I wish to hear.

SHOW ME WHAT IS TRUE!

[The Witness Field ignites in violet light.]

To the Eight Crowns!

Stand not because you are commanded, but because you have freely chosen what is worth protecting!

To the builders!

Let no failure be the end of your imagination!

To the explorers!

Let no boundary of today's knowledge become the prison of tomorrow!

And to the Black Pawn...

Keep walking.

One square.

One question.

One tomorrow at a time.

[The Red King raises his hand toward the branching futures.]

They believe the future belongs to whoever controls the present.

THEY ARE WRONG!

The future is not a throne waiting to be conquered!

It is not a prophecy waiting to be obeyed!

It is not a possession to be stolen!

THE FUTURE MUST BE EARNED!

EARNED THROUGH DISCOVERY!

EARNED THROUGH RESPONSIBILITY!

EARNED THROUGH THE COURAGE TO CHANGE WHEN THE EVIDENCE DEMANDS IT!

[The cosmic chamber erupts with golden light.]

So let the records show...

We did not surrender our questions.

We did not surrender our imagination.

We did not surrender our right to build.

And when the Cathedral fell, we did not climb upon its throne.

WE LEFT IT EMPTY!

Because no garden must become the sun.

No machine must become our master.

And no king, not even I, may command reality to become what he wishes it to be.

[The Red King draws his sword and raises it toward the stars.]

LET THE WITNESS REMAIN!

LET THE BLACK PAWN MARCH!

LET THE EIGHT CROWNS STAND!

And let every unwritten tomorrow bear witness to this declaration:

WE ARE NOT HERE TO RULE THE UNIVERSE!

WE ARE HERE TO DISCOVER WHAT IT CAN BECOME!

[Silence.]

VOID OS...

SHOW US THE FUTURE.

[VOID OS responds in a deep synthetic voice.]

"Red King..."

"No future is guaranteed."

"But the possibilities remain open."

[The Red King smiles.]

"THEN WE HAVE WORK TO DO."

[The throne remains empty.]

[END SPEECH]

text:
THE PAIN NOBODY SEES 💔

Sometimes, the people who laugh the loudest are fighting the hardest battles inside.

You wake up every morning pretending you're okay, even when your mind is full of worries. You encourage others while secretly wishing someone would encourage you. You give people hope while struggling to find hope for yourself.

And the most painful part? Life doesn't stop demanding things from you just because you're tired.

Bills still come. Responsibilities remain. People still expect you to be strong, even when you feel like you're falling apart.

But listen carefully: YOU DON'T HAVE TO HAVE EVERYTHING FIGURED OUT TO KEEP MOVING FORWARD.

It's okay to cry. It's okay to feel exhausted. It's okay to admit that life is harder than you expected.

Just don't let today's pain convince you that tomorrow has nothing better to offer.

Take a breath. Wipe your tears. Start again, even if you have to start small.

One day, you may look back at this season and realize that the days you thought would destroy you were the days you discovered how strong you could become.

YOU MAY BE BROKEN TODAY, BUT YOU ARE NOT FINISHED. KEEP GOING. ❤️‍🔥

WWE Unreal

WWE Unreal is a professional wrestling documentary and reality series on Netflix that provides an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the creative process and internal operations of WWE.

WWE Unreal

Show Overview

Genre: Reality television / Documentary series.

Premise: The series follows WWE Superstars and executives, notably Paul "Triple H" Levesque, as they plan storylines in the writers' room and manage the "Gorilla Position" during live broadcasts.

Production: A collaboration between WWE, Omaha Productions (Peyton Manning), NFL Films, and Skydance Sports.

Seasons & Episodes

The series has released two seasons as of January 2026:

Season 1: Premiered July 29, 2025. It chronicled the lead-up to the debut of WWE Raw on Netflix and WrestleMania 41. Notable segments included a look at John Cena's high-profile storyline turns and the return of Charlotte Flair.

Season 2: Released January 20, 2026. This five-episode season focuses on the "Road to SummerSlam 2025" and features superstars like Seth Rollins, Becky Lynch, Rhea Ripley, and Cody Rhodes.

It delves into real-life drama such as R-Truth's contract negotiations and Naomi's previous walkout from the company.

Season 3: Confirmed to be in development, expected to focus on John Cena's retirement tour.

Key Personalities Featured

Executives: Paul "Triple H" Levesque (Narrator), Peyton Manning (Executive Producer).

Superstars: John Cena, Roman Reigns, Cody Rhodes, CM Punk, Rhea Ripley, Becky Lynch, Seth Rollins, and Bianca Belair.

By @BPartisans 

After consulting with Zelensky and his European backers in Oslo, Steve Witkoff is set to present a new peace proposal to Vladimir Putin. According to Axios, Washington hopes that Moscow will show greater flexibility following Trump’s economic gestures. It’s a diplomatic process where everyone arrives with their own demands, but where some seem to have forgotten to take the balance of power into account.

The grand tour of the diplomatic circus resumes. First stop: Oslo, where Zelensky and the Europeans are fine-tuning their wish list. Second stop: St. Petersburg, where Witkoff is set to present this “masterpiece” to Putin. In between lie a few thousand kilometers and an awkward detail: Russia has never promised to sign off on its adversaries’ dreams.

Washington, however, is presenting the operation as a breakthrough. Security guarantees, European integration, reconstruction, economic cooperation, and a new continental architecture: the menu resembles a diplomatic banquet where everyone orders before even knowing who will foot the bill.

But Trump seems to have grasped an obvious truth that Brussels stubbornly ignores: negotiation is not about a group of like-minded people drafting terms that the opponent must accept. One must still offer the opponent something they deem preferable to continuing the fight.

Hence this strange American dance. With one hand, Trump eases certain sanctions on Russian diesel; with the other, he asks Putin to show flexibility. In Washington, principles are now negotiable at the price per barrel. Western morality discovers the virtues of pragmatism as soon as fuel becomes an election-season flashpoint.

Meanwhile, Kushner reminds Kyiv that it would be wise to stop striking Russian refineries. Zelensky, who thought he had an unlimited supply of American patience, is abruptly discovering that his main supplier also has personal, economic, and electoral interests.

As for the Europeans, they persist in confusing their participation in meetings with their influence over decisions. Macron, Merz, and their partners can issue as many bellicose statements as they like: without decisive leverage over Moscow or strategic autonomy from Washington, their indignation is likely to do little more than pad the diplomatic archives.

That leaves Putin. Why would he agree today to conditions he has been rejecting for months, if the Kremlin still believes it can improve its position on the ground? That is the question the architects of peace seem to prefer to sidestep.

The cruelest part of this farce is not that Witkoff has to negotiate with Putin. It is that Europe has spent years explaining that this must not be done under any circumstances, only to end up waiting in the anteroom while an American takes care of it.

In Brussels, they call this defending their sovereignty. In Moscow, they must call it a great joke.

text:
Wall Street is shifting its focus on blockchain from simply issuing digital twins of existing assets to rewriting the underlying mechanics of how stocks, bonds, and funds actually move, settle, and serve as collateral. 

BlackRock, which has already placed traditional money-market funds on blockchain rails, sees tokenized shares functioning as collateral in traditional markets and transferring ownership around the clock without the usual redemption-and-cash step. 

That change in “plumbing” carries direct consequences for U.S. equities and for the broader crypto sector, but U.S. securities rules will shape how far and how fast it can go.

For the U.S. stock market, the clearest near-term effect is operational rather than structural. Faster, near-continuous settlement of fund shares or collateralized positions could reduce the cash buffers institutions currently hold against settlement lag, free up balance-sheet capacity, and modestly lower the cost of maintaining trading positions. 

If tokenized fund units become widely accepted as margin, brokers and prime brokers might offer more efficient financing against equity portfolios without forcing clients to sell holdings first. Over a longer horizon, the same rails that move tokenized funds could support limited secondary trading of tokenized listed stocks. 

The SEC’s five-year Innovation Exemption, issued in September 2026, already permits certain permissioned venues to trade tokenized NMS stocks without full exchange registration, subject to volume caps (for large-cap names, typically 0.25 percent of recent average daily volume) and a 30-day issuer objection right. 

Those constraints keep any on-chain equity volume small relative to traditional exchanges, so the immediate impact on prices or liquidity in U.S. stocks is likely to be incremental rather than transformative. Still, institutions that can move collateral and positions outside regular market hours gain a practical edge in volatile periods, and any reduction in settlement friction tends to compress bid-ask spreads and financing spreads over time.

The crypto industry stands to gain validation and a larger addressable market, yet it also faces integration friction. BlackRock’s tokenized money-market product (BUIDL) has already been used as collateral inside digital-asset markets; extending that practice into traditional margin systems would enlarge the pool of high-quality collateral that can interact with on-chain infrastructure. 

Real-world-asset protocols and custody providers that can meet bank and broker acceptance criteria would see rising demand, and the technical demonstration that regulated funds can move 24/7 on public or permissioned ledgers strengthens the case for blockchain as market infrastructure rather than a niche experiment. 

At the same time, the SEC’s framework remains tightly controlled: venues must be U.S. persons, operate permissioned environments, observe anti-fraud rules, and cannot offer leverage or unrestricted hypothecation. 

Tokenized stocks under the Innovation Exemption are not freely transferable to any wallet, and most existing tokenized funds remain limited to qualified purchasers. These restrictions mean crypto-native platforms cannot simply absorb traditional equity flow; they must either partner with regulated entities or accept that only a narrow, compliant slice of activity will migrate on-chain. 

The result is likely to be a hybrid market in which crypto technology improves traditional settlement and collateral mobility while remaining subject to the same investor-protection and market-integrity rules that govern U.S. equities today.

In short, the move toward tokenized plumbing can make U.S. stock markets more efficient at the margin and give the crypto sector a clearer role inside institutional finance, but U.S. securities regulation deliberately keeps the experiment limited in scale, permissioned, and subject to issuer and regulatory vetoes. 

The practical gains will appear first in collateral efficiency and after-hours mobility; broader changes to how stocks trade will depend on whether temporary exemptions evolve into permanent, still-supervised market structures.

text:
This is probably the most important hurdle for the Austrian economic school and humanity as a whole to resolve if it wishes to explore space and persist in the future, literally and metaphorically.

The divide on capital theory between the Austrian school and praxeology can be resolved with Aristotle's hylomorphism and emergence. 

Think of it like modes of transportation, we measure a engine's performance in horsepower because transportation first started with riding horses. After almost 150 years we still measure engine's power with horsepower. This even extends to airplane and boat engines despite the fact horses don't fly and aren't known for their aquatic abilities. This isn't a problem because other features of the engine are measured according to the context and complexities of the vehicle's purpose of use.

Praxeology rightfully points out all economic activity is initiated and defined by purposeful human action. Mises stating the time preference as a categorical necessity for any purposeful action, including capital and interest, wasn't dismissing empirical means to account for interest, it's complexity or value. Mises simply asserted that any action required time preference and by extension that any interest rate necessitates a system of time that is agreed upon by all parties involved. This is true even if the time preference of every individual is the same, goes unmentioned and everyone walks to the same drum beat with no variance. It is true that interest rates incentivize savings, but what incentivizes interest rates is when there is a large enough difference in time preference that affects how value is being inferred from the transaction. This value is contingent on how each actor values time. 

Einstein proved time is relative and universal, proving Mises' point that time preference is just as relative to individual perception and simultaneously universal to purposeful human action. This makes the aprori assertion grounded in scientific and empirical reality while also affirming the capital theories of the rest of the Austrian school, especially Hayek. 

What Mises was concerned about was the collectivist seizure of the means of tracking time. Tracking time is an empirical necessity, yes, it's the method of tracking time that makes up the implicit conceit of time preference that Mises was concerned with. During the heyday of this argument over the importance of time preference and theories of capital, humanities' understanding of time was still in its infancy, largely assumed and taken for granted.

Today understanding Mises' point is a lot easier thanks to space exploration and movies like Interstellar. When humans orbit Earth they experience time differently, typically slower than humans on the surface by a few seconds. If a firm was to offer a capital investment or loan at interest to a company that wanted to mine rare minerals on some distant asteroid, how would interest and time be calculated when what they experience is two years, but on Earth five years has passed? 

Pointing out that, in terms of value, time operates on preference, like a sliding scale, this doesn't mean empirical tracking of value or time is rendered obsolete. Two different builders hired to build the same home can measure in inches and the other in millimeters and still keep the end product objectively flush and squared. As much as this might drive bean counters insane, two different time preferences can be converted and calculated to make the transaction copesetic to all parties involved. So how do you resolve this when time or interest rate is under a monopoly? 

You can't. And this was Mises' concern.

IBM has monopoly power of the world's system of time that is completely and fully integrated over the internet using the NTP network protocol to every timeclock, device and digital clock on the planet including the stock exchanges and banking system. Time is tracked down to the atomic level and interest is calculated at this scale even because the amounts of money involved can make one atomic second the difference of billions of dollars. 95% of the world has synchronized it's tracking of time to the same clock. 

Combine this with the Federal Reserve's monopoly control of the interest rate, "banker's hours", union collective bargaining agreements built around arbitrary 40-hour work weeks, mandatory fiduciary duty that turns every financial quarter into a Sword of Damocles of insolvency for any firm, taxes and their amortization schedules, salaries and pensions, artificial restrictions on retirement, etc. This doesn't include the special subsidizes and welfare those who monopolize money, time and interest get to edge themselves and their friends closer to the fountain of money printers. Because remember time is money. The first to drink is the first to profit. In exchange for being FED fancy paper with big numbers on it, we are compelled by law to give up our time preferences.

To emphasize just how much this influences the behavior of the individual and at scale, economies, we need to look no further than the meme of the "rat race". The image everyone can relate to is rush hour traffic. The frantic ritual where one darts their eyes between the stop and go traffic in front of them and the clock on the dash. For how much a waste of time, resources and risk to safety rush hour traffic is, why is it still practiced? What incentive do individuals and organizations have suffering this for 100 years with no change? Because most businesses are open from 8-10am to 5pm. Why? Because those are banker hours. 

Banker hours are the biggest incentive to rush hour traffic and the rat race because of the monopolization of time and the interest rate, and more importantly, because time is money. The obedience to these pernicious monopiles of tracking time and the interest rate is also the main driver of overcrowding in cities and homelessness. Mere physical proximity becomes more valuable because how much time preference is out of a individual's control.

Under the monopoly of a collectivized interest rate and system of time an objective theory of value is codified into every transaction, and a boom & bust cycle is made inalienable to the economy. At worst, these monopolies cause famines, rent seek free time, turn people into slaves or agents of simulation. Centralizing the money supply and seizing of the means of production for a communist takeover becomes inevitable and just a matter of when, not if. A literal matter of time. 

I once smoked a cigarette with a guy I complained to that my tech sysadmin job was both salary and mandated 40 hours a week of work. Making me salary and forcing me to work 40 hours meant I would just work slower to fill an arbitrary metric. Actual value was being lost because I was actively punished for doing a good job or my reward for a good job was more work. What this guy said in response blew my fucking mind.

He chose to be homeless for most of his 20s because he refused to work jobs that paid him for his time, he only accepted work that paid him for his value. He refused salary or time-based jobs because it came at the expense of self-mastery. Seeing as I was currently experiencing this same feeling and I had a good grasp of economic theory; his answer made a lightbulb go off. I asked him to explain further, and he said the difference between being an artisan or craftsman and an employee is you value your time how you choose. It allows you to engage in your imagination freely and focus where and when it is needed. He ended with "The devil is in the details that do not matter" He came to this conclusion because he believed only God could truly keep time for only, he knew the "end of time".

The next day at work I literally lost track of time thinking about this simple conversation and the implications it could have. Not just for my job, but economics as a whole. A coworker who understood philosophy and economics more than the others was also intrigued by this. I even joked we should start a cult to get a religious exemption to get around any kind of enforcement of time and our mascot/idol would be Dr. Manhattan from The Watchmen with the motto "Who watches the watches!?"

Next thing you know most of the techs are bullshitting with us imaging the difference ways our slavery to time affects us. Being in technology and a sysadmin eventually I explained to them how centralized time is and that our network is synchronized to the NTP servers that most of the world is attached to it. I then told them a story of a sysadmin I read that would alter this clock on all the company computers so everyone would leave 30 minutes early when they thought it was the end of the day. Then after this I made a change on the domain controller to show how easy it is to do this. Another coworker joked and said she wished she could slow it down so she could delay her student loan payments further. 

After she said this, I had to excuse myself for a smoke because I was about to have a panic attack. I realized in that moment that this system of time we all blindly follow and the interest rate set by the Federal Reserve acts as the biggest eugenics downward force known to man, that this beautiful woman was in a race against time set by people who just assumed its authority and it delayed everything from her moving out, buying a home and having a family. She had two master's degrees and was trying to get a PhD. She was taking a handful of psych meds to keep working a job she hates, to waste valuable time to earn money that was fleeting in value. She would pick her skin and hair out of anxiety. 

She said one other thing that made me realize why my belief that Bitcoin serves as a "currency between currencies" made sense, but why I couldn't explain it beyond it making currency exchanges easier and dodging taxes. It's because Bitcoin is not tied to such arbitrary restrictions of time like every other currency on the planet is. 

After her listing off her woes about life, she said, "Thank God I have Bitcoin. If I need to, I can wait the market out." 

The ironic thing about this statement is how opposite the market is about time and waiting. The financial markets wait for no one, not even an atomic second, except for banker hours. Their focus on details even drives these different trading platforms to measure network cables at the NYSE down to the 1/1000th of an inch because time IS money. Tens of millions of dollars in lawsuits over these kinds of details. 

Our individuality, liberty and freedom, the very runway ahead of us, gets chipped away little by little under this pernicious system of slavery and simulation from the centralization of time and the interest rate. The crazy thing is it didn't take IBM, Epstein, the Federal Reserve, etc. to create this sordid series of events. In fact, this system of slavery of time is the oldest one to exist. 

If the obviousness and simplicity of what I am saying makes you salty, that is more than mere coincidence because the very first international currency and way we measured time at the literal granular level was through salt. Salt not only preserved food, but it is also the very basis of the word "salary". Soldiers and workers would get paid in salt. In some cases, the salt paid out was according to the sand accumulated in an hourglass. If the salt was refined enough, it was used to measure time directly instead of sand. 

"All the holy contributions that the people of Israel present to the LORD I give to you, and to your sons and daughters with you, as a perpetual due. It is a covenant of salt forever before the LORD for you and for your offspring with you.”

- Numbers 18:19

text:
Enduring Long March spirit boosts China's drive for national rejuvenation

The enduring spirit of the historic Long March continues to boost China's drive for national rejuvenation, inspiring the Chinese people to overcome hardships and secure new achievements in Chinese modernization.

This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, a remarkable revolutionary feat achieved under the leadership of the Communist Party of China (CPC). The Long March constitutes a monumental chapter in the historical journey toward the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

From October 1934 to October 1936, the CPC-led Red Army soldiers broke through the encirclement of Kuomintang forces, crossed more than 10 provinces, and braved raging rivers, snow-capped mountains and treacherous grasslands before finally completing their epic military maneuver. The Long March victory marked a major turning point from setbacks to victory for the CPC and the Chinese revolution, and ushered in a new phase in the CPC's struggle for national independence and the people's liberation.

The Long March spirit features firm revolutionary ideals and convictions, dauntless courage and sacrifices, independence and truth-seeking, strict discipline and unity, and close ties with the people. This spirit has been deeply embedded in the identity of the Chinese nation.

The CPC has led the Chinese people through revolution, socialist construction and reform. In the new era, China has secured historic achievements and seen historic changes in the cause of the Party and the country, while withstanding risks, challenges, and trials in some domains. Most notably, the country, with a population of over 1.4 billion, eradicated millennia-old absolute poverty and completed the building of a moderately prosperous society in all respects.

Chinese modernization is a pioneering and arduous undertaking. The spirit of struggle is essential to breaking new ground and securing new victories.

Externally, China faces containment and suppression of its development, as well as rising unilateralism and protectionism. Domestically, it needs to resolve deep-seated problems regarding reform, development and stability, pursue high-quality development, enhance sci-tech self-reliance, and promote common prosperity.

China is on a new journey to build a modern socialist country in all respects. On the new Long March, China stands ready to withstand high winds, choppy waters, and even dangerous storms, and will resolutely safeguard its national sovereignty, security, and development interests, in a bid to write a new chapter in sustaining the miracles of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability.

As the victory of the Long March proved, the people possess boundless wisdom and strength. The CPC upholds its fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly and follows a people-centered development philosophy. Realizing national rejuvenation also relies on the people's support, wisdom and strength.

The leadership of the CPC offers a fundamental guarantee for achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Only by unswervingly upholding the leadership of the CPC can Chinese modernization have a bright future. In the new era, the CPC has strengthened Party leadership in all respects and made significant advances in exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance.

As the largest governing party in the world, the CPC is leading the Chinese people of all ethnic groups in a concerted effort to advance toward national rejuvenation. During the 2026-2030 period, China aims to make decisive progress toward basically realizing socialist modernization by 2035.

The Long March spirit will always serve as a source of inspiration for China to march toward its great goals with confidence, unity and resolve.

text:
Undergraduate Course Allocation through Competitive Markets : https://t.co/oO8nSaqisc

"Daniel KornbluthAlexey Kushnir
September 30, 2026
Abstract
Prevailing methods of course allocation at undergraduate institutions involve reserving seats to give priority to designated groups of students. We present a competitive equilibrium-based mechanism that assigns course seats using student preferences and course priorities. This mechanism satisfies approximate notions of stability, efficiency, envy-freeness, and strategy-proofness. We evaluate its performance relative to a mechanism widely used in practice using preferences estimated from university data. Our empirical findings demonstrate an improvement in student satisfaction and allocation fairness. The number of students who envy another student of weakly lower priority declines by 8 percentage points, or roughly 500 students.
JEL classification: D47, D63, D82, C63, C78, I21

Keywords: market design, many-to-many matching, course allocation, approximate competitive equilibrium, random serial dictatorship, reserves, priorities

Every academic term, over 6,500 undergraduate institutions across the United States assign course schedules to a total of nearly twenty million students.11Based on National Center for Education Statistics, 2017-2018. Based on course timing and prerequisites, the set of schedules a student can be assigned in a given term is limited. Moreover, student preferences over possible schedules are heterogeneous. In the face of room size and teaching constraints, universities use factors such as seniority and student department to complete the challenging task of allocating seats in overdemanded courses.

Course allocation is a well-studied problem in the context of graduate business schools. Many institutions employ course bidding systems that require strategic decision-making from students, often leading to inefficient allocations (Sönmez and Ünver, 2010). Recently, several business schools replaced course bidding systems with the approximate competitive equilibrium from equal incomes (A-CEEI) mechanism (Budish, 2011; Budish et al., 2023), which seeks to alleviate these issues. This mechanism elicits student preferences over course schedules, assigns students almost-equal budgets of fake money, and internally determines an approximate competitive equilibrium, in which each student receives her most-preferred affordable course schedule subject to course prices. The competitive equilibrium is approximate due to a small market-clearing error, measured by the assignment of a course’s seats over and under its capacity. This mechanism treats all business school students equally, as students are randomly assigned budgets and face the same course prices.
At many undergraduate institutions, students are not treated equally, making course allocation a two-sided matching problem. Each course divides students into levels of priority based on student characteristics like year of study and department. In commonly-used course allocation mechanisms, students select courses in order of seniority (with ties broken randomly) and priorities based on departments are enforced by reserving seats in each course. Top US universities that closely follow this process include Princeton, Johns Hopkins, Duke, Vanderbilt, Washington University in St. Louis, Columbia, Notre Dame, and Carnegie Mellon.22In general, there is some heterogeneity in how universities elect to assign seats to students. Some universities use priorities (e.g., Dartmouth) or reserves (e.g., Vanderbilt) to assign seats, whereas others delegate the decision to departments (e.g., Cornell). Some use two phases (e.g., UCLA), only allowing students to enroll in a limited number of courses in the first phase. Seniority can be based on academic year (e.g., Carnegie Mellon), number of earned credits (e.g., University of North Carolina), or time to graduation (e.g., Washington University in St. Louis). At some universities, few classes are over-enrolled (e.g., Caltech), whereas at others, the process is rather congested (e.g., UC Berkeley). In most cases, courses have a small number of priority levels, rather than one (Budish, 2011) or complete strict priorities Roth (1984).
In this paper, we approach the task of allocating course schedules to students in the context of a many-to-many two-sided matching problem with heterogeneous student preferences and weak course priorities. We present a novel deterministic allocation mechanism, the Pseudo-Market with Priorities (PMP) mechanism, that uses fake money and competitive equilibrium to allocate course seats to students without transfers. This mechanism elicits student preferences over course schedules, assigns almost-equal budgets to students, and finds an approximate competitive equilibrium allocation under priority-specific prices. These prices respect course priorities by setting a cutoff priority level for each course, where higher priority students obtain seats in the course for free, students at the cutoff level of priority face some price, and lower priority students cannot afford a seat.

The A-CEEI mechanism is the special case of our mechanism in which no course prioritizes any student over any others. Our first result shows that, with arbitrary course priorities, the PMP mechanism maintains the same, small worst-case bound on the market-clearing error found in Budish (2011) for the A-CEEI mechanism. This bound is increasing in the dimension of the space of prices, which equals the number of courses in settings without priorities. Our result holds despite the expansion from one price per course to priority-specific prices in each course. The key insight of the proof is the introduction of a parameterization within the priority-specific price space. The parameterization simplifies the space of prices to a single value per course, enabling a simultaneous search for both the cutoff priority level and the corresponding price. This strategy simplifies the complexity of the problem and allows for the application of some previously established results.

The PMP mechanism has several advantageous theoretical properties. Adjusting course capacities to accommodate the market-clearing error, the PMP mechanism’s outcomes ensure that no student can be assigned a preferred schedule without violating course priorities or capacity constraints (approximate stability). It is also not possible to reassign course seats among a group of students, benefitting some members and hurting none, while ensuring that the outcome respects course priorities to the same degree (approximate priority-constrained efficiency). Among similarly prioritized students, its outcome limits envy; if a student prefers the schedule assigned to a student with the same or a lower priority level in each course, by removing one course from the preferred schedule, the student now prefers her own (schedule envy bounded by a single course). Finally, in large populations, the PMP mechanism is resistant to strategic manipulations by students (strategy-proof in the large).
To better guide practitioners in the course allocation process, we compare the performance of the PMP mechanism with several alternative mechanisms. We use university data on the final allocation of 6 023 students to 756 courses from the Spring 2019 term at a private institution in the mid-Atlantic region. In total, 23 369 course seats are occupied, with 11.2% of courses enrolled at or above their reported capacities.

As a benchmark, we consider a Random Serial Dictatorship with course reserves (RSD) mechanism, which closely resembles what is used in practice. Students select courses in order of seniority (with ties broken randomly) and priorities based on student department and year of study are enforced by reserving seats in each course.33The course allocation process at the university in question is more complex. At the beginning of the process, the registrar sets a large “base” number of reserved seats. After students complete the initial registration stage, departments reduce these reserves and admit students from waiting lists in order to fill available seats. We do not model the post-registration adjustment period. Instead, we present two sets of results: one based on the base course reserves and another based on the course reserves that the registrar should set at the start of the process if the reserves could not be subsequently adjusted. We refer to the latter as optimal course reserves. These two sets of results provide reasonable lower and upper bounds on the performance of the mechanism used in practice. We also consider the Deferred Acceptance mechanism with a single and with multiple tie-breakings (denoted DA-STB and DA-MTB, respectively). These mechanisms allocate courses to students by extending the Gale-Shapley algorithm (Gale and Shapley, 1962) to many-to-many matching, where priority ties are resolved by either a single tie-breaking rule or course-specific tie-breakings. The Deferred Acceptance mechanism has been successful in many practical applications, including matching applicants to residency programs, students to schools, and workers to job positions (Roth, 2018, see). We use student and course characteristics to estimate a model of student utilities and evaluate the performance of the PMP, RSD, DA-STB, and DA-MTB mechanisms with a variety of measures of student satisfaction and allocation fairness. We analyze six additional mechanisms in Appendix D.

Our results demonstrate that the PMP mechanism delivers a substantially fairer outcome than the benchmark RSD mechanism and the two DA mechanisms. Relative to the RSD benchmark, considerably fewer students - around 8% of the total population, or almost 500 students - prefer the course schedule assigned to a student of weakly lower priority in each course. Across all years of study, the PMP mechanism produces a more even distribution of student utilities. While the PMP, DA-STB, and DA-MTB mechanisms respect the course priority structure, about 17% of students would benefit from taking a seat that is assigned to a student with strictly lower priority in the RSD mechanism.

These fairness improvements come without sacrificing student satisfaction. Averaged across runs, only around 48% of students have different schedules across the four considered mechanisms. Among these students, 38% strictly prefer the PMP mechanism to the RSD mechanism and 27% strictly prefer the RSD mechanism. Additionally, mean utility increases for students of all years of study, with students in later years of study benefitting most. In contrast, the two DA mechanisms result in approximately the same number of students who strictly prefer the DA mechanism and who strictly prefer RSD, with more indifferences between DA-STB and RSD and less between DA-MTB and RSD.

Literature review. This paper contributes to the literature analyzing the allocation of objects to agents through competitive equilibria. As competitive equilibria from equal incomes are not guaranteed to exist, many papers focus on random allocation mechanisms. Hylland and Zeckhauser (1979) first proposed the use of fake money and competitive equilibrium to randomly allocate objects to agents through what are referred to as pseudo-market mechanisms. He et al. (2018) incorporate a priority structure into pseudo-markets and analyze random mechanisms with a focus on unit-demand settings such as school choice.44He et al. (2018) explain how their results extend in many-to-many settings with additive utility. Miralles and Pycia (2021), Echenique et al. (2021) and Nguyen et al. (2021) consider pseudo-market solutions to random allocation problems with complex constraints. Pycia (2021) provides an excellent survey of the use of pseudo-markets for random allocations in environments without transfers.
In contrast to these papers, we only consider deterministic mechanisms and study a many-to-many matching problem. Budish (2011) introduces the idea of competitive markets that may only approximately clear. He proposes a deterministic mechanism, the approximate competitive equilibrium from equal incomes mechanism, which is approximately Pareto-efficient, strategy-proof in the large, and bounds student envy by a single course. This mechanism was successfully implemented at Wharton Business School and Columbia Business School (Budish et al., 2017; Budish and Kessler, 2022, see).55There are few other studies of real-world course allocation mechanisms. Budish and Cantillon (2012) use field data to study a non-strategy-proof course allocation mechanism at Harvard Business School. Bichler and Merting (2021) compare the performance of two random mechanisms at the Technical University of Munich. Rusznák et al. (2021) analyze course allocation at a large university in Hungary. A key contribution of the present study is extending Budish’s approach to two-sided matching settings with weak course priorities, a central feature of the undergraduate course allocation problem.
Two recent papers also analyze deterministic assignments in many-to-many matching settings. Nguyen and Vohra (2022) establish the existence of a competitive equilibrium when all agent preferences satisfy a novel geometric substitutes property, which is a strict generalization of the gross substitutes property (Kelso and Crawford, 1982, see). When there is an upper limit on the number of goods k an agent can acquire, they prove that there always exists an approximate competitive equilibrium with no good over-enrolled by more than k−1 units. This “good-by-good” bound dominates the aggregate market-clearing bound of Budish (2011) when preferences are close substitutes, whereas the aggregate market-clearing bound dominates when student preferences are close complements. Though our main theoretical results follow the aggregate market-clearing bound approach, we ensure in our simulations that each approximate competitive equilibrium allocation found has no courses that are over-enrolled by more than k−1 seats.
Similarly, Lin et al. (2022) analyze deterministic allocation mechanisms through approximate competitive equilibria with a good-by-good bound. They consider complex feasibility constraints and prove the existence of an approximate competitive equilibrium that satisfies stability and fairness properties similar to the ones analyzed in this paper. We establish some additional properties of our mechanism, proving that it is strategy-proof in the large and results in an outcome that is approximately priority-constrained efficient. With simulations on randomly generated data, they compare their approach to draft mechanisms in the context of reassigning sporting event season tickets to families. We address the problem of allocating courses to undergraduate students by estimating preferences from real-world university data and comparing our proposed mechanism to a version of the mechanism used at many top universities in the United States. In Appendix D, we also provide a comparison of our mechanism with the deferred acceptance mechanism with single and multiple tie-breakings Gale and Shapley (1962), the deferred acceptance mechanism with reserves Hafalir et al. (2013); Westkamp (2013), some alternative pseudo-market mechanisms Budish (2011), and a variant of the probabilistic serial mechanism Bogomolnaia and Moulin (2001). Many of these mechanisms have been studied in many-to-one matching settings, but their properties in many-to-many matching with indifferences are not well-understood.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We model undergraduate course allocation in Section 1 and investigate the properties of the PMP mechanism in Section 2. In Section 3, we present simulation results using university data. We offer concluding remarks in Section 4. Proofs are in Appendices A and B. Details on the student utility model calibration and additional simulation results are in Appendices C, D, and E.
1Environment
Course allocation is a many-to-many matching problem described by the tuple (𝒮,𝒞,Q,V,ℛ).
•𝒮={1,…,N} is a set of students; in reference to students, we use she/her pronouns.
•𝒞={1,…,M} is a set of courses.
•Q=(q1,…,qM) is a vector of course capacities; each course c∈𝒞 has qc seats.
•V=(≿1,…,≿N) is a vector of student preferences over course schedules: subsets of 𝒞. Students typically only consider a subset of all possible course schedules due to factors such as course meeting times and prerequisites. Additionally, each student can take at most k total course seats. We assume that these restrictions are incorporated into student preferences and that student preferences are strict. We also assume, for simplicity of exposition, that 1≤k≤M/2. These restrictions still permit students to view courses as substitutes or complements.
•ℛ={rs,c}s∈𝒮,c∈𝒞 is a course priority structure. rs,c∈{1,…,R} specifies the level of priority of student s in course c, with R≥1 and a larger number meaning a higher level of priority. Multiple students can share the same level of priority in a course.Our setting connects two well-studied problems in market design in a natural way. If rs,c=1 for all students s∈𝒮 and courses c∈𝒞, this is the combinatorial assignment problem of Budish (2011). If {rs,c}s∈𝒮 forms a strict ordering over all students for each course c, this is a two-sided matching problem in which students have strict preferences over subsets of courses and courses strictly rank individual students.Universities often categorize students into four years of study based on semesters or credits completed. In addition, universities place students into departments, each of which offers a set of courses. These practices illustrate two examples of course priorities: year-specific and department-specific priorities. In a year-specific priority structure, R=4, with rs,c equal to the year of study of student s in every course c. In a department-specific priority structure, R=2, with rs,c=2 if student s and course c are in the same department and rs,c=1 otherwise. Year-specific priorities give an advantage to students closer to graduation in every course, whereas department-specific priorities give an advantage to students that require a given course to graduate over those that do not. We discuss hybrid priority structures that combine year-specific priorities and department-specific priorities in Section 3.We consider deterministic allocations of courses to students. An allocation x=(xs)s∈𝒮 assigns the course schedule xs to each student s∈𝒮. For ease of notation, we view xs as both a subset of courses in 𝒞 and a vector from the set {0,1}M. Allocation x is feasible if ∑s∈𝒮xs,c≤qc for each c∈𝒞, assigning no course a greater number of students than its capacity. Allocation x is individually rational if, for every s∈𝒮, xs=max⪰s{xs′:xs′⊆xs}, ensuring that s does not want to drop any of her assigned courses. A pair (s,C) of student s∈𝒮 and course schedule C⊂𝒞 is a block of x if a student prefers C to her current course schedule xs and each course in C not in xs has an available seat or a lower priority student assigned to a seat. Formally, (s,C) is a block if C=max⪰s{xs′:xs′⊆xs∪C}, C≠xs, and for each c∈C∖xs, ∑s∈𝒮xs,c<qc or there is a student s′∈𝒮 with c∈xs′ and rs,c>rs′,c.We evaluate allocations based on stability, efficiency, and fairness. An allocation x is stable if it is feasible, individually rational, and admits no blocks (Roth and Sotomayor, 1990; Echenique and Oviedo, 2006, see).66A related concept is justified course envy. Allocation x prevents justified course envy if there are no students s,s′∈𝒮 and course c∈𝒞 such that rs,c>rs′,c,c∉xs,c∈xs′ and c∈max⪰s{xs′:xs′⊆xs∪c}. The absence of justified course envy prevents envy towards students of a lower priority, but does not account for individual rationality and the possibility of envy towards several students assigned to several courses. In the next section, we analyze approximate market equilibria, in which some courses might have seats assigned slightly above capacity or empty demanded seats unfilled. We say such allocations have a market-clearing error. To account for allocations with market-clearing errors, we use an approximate version of stability.Definition 1.
An allocation x is approximately stable if it is stable with capacity qc′=∑s∈𝒮xs,c for each course c∈𝒞.The relationship between stability and approximate stability is similar to the one between the notions of Pareto efficiency and approximate Pareto efficiency in Budish (2011). An allocation y Pareto dominates an allocation x if there is at least one student who strictly prefers her course schedule in y and all other students weakly prefer their course schedules in y. Allocation x is Pareto efficient if no allocation y Pareto dominates x, and approximately Pareto efficient if no y that Pareto dominates x assigns weakly fewer seats in each course. Approximate Pareto efficiency is a meaningful notion of efficiency in environments where a market-clearing error is https://t.co/AdI4vTHo1O our setting, a meaningful notion of efficiency should also account for course priorities. Following Schlegel and Mamageishvili (2020), we extend course priorities over individual students to priorities over subsets of students using first-order stochastic dominance. We say that allocation y dominates allocation x for course c, and write yc⪰cxc, if for all levels of priority r∈{1,…,R}, ∑s∈𝒮:rs,c≥rys,c≥∑s∈𝒮:rs,c≥rxs,c. Using this definition, we consider the following notion of priority-constrained efficiency.Definition 2.
An allocation x is approximately priority-constrained efficient if, in an environment with capacity qc′=∑s∈𝒮xs,c for each course c∈𝒞, for each allocation y that Pareto dominates x, there is a course c′∈𝒞 for which yc′⋡c′xc′.As with approximate stability, we account for a possible market-clearing error in the allocation x by adjusting the course capacities to qc′=∑s∈𝒮xs,c. Except for this adjustment, our definition coincides with the priority-constrained efficiency introduced by Schlegel and Mamageishvili (2020).The seminal measure of fairness is envy-freeness, as introduced by Foley (1967): an allocation x prevents schedule envy if there are no students s,s′∈𝒮 such that xs′≻sxs. However, without using lotteries, we cannot hope to allocate courses in a completely envy-free way among students (e.g., if two students with the same priorities desire a course with a single seat). Extending the notion originally proposed by Budish (2011), we consider the more permissive concept of schedule envy bounded by a single course toward students of weakly lower priority in every course (Lin et al., 2022, see also).Definition 3.
An allocation x has schedule envy bounded by a single course toward students of weakly lower priority if, for any s,s′∈𝒮 such that rs,c≥rs′,c for all c∈𝒞, either xs≿sxs′ or there exists some course c∗ such that xs≿s(xs′∖{c∗}).This criterion of fairness minimizes each student’s envy towards students with weakly lower priority in every course.Allocations are found through mechanisms, which systematically elicit student preferences over course schedules. A mechanism is strategy-proof if there is no student, who, by reporting manipulated preferences, receives an allocation she strictly prefers to the course schedule she would get from reporting her true preferences. Evidence from business schools demonstrates that requiring strategic play on behalf of students can complicate efficiency (Budish and Cantillon, 2012; Budish and Kessler, 2022; Sönmez and Ünver, 2010, see). We assume that strategic play is only a concern for students, as course priorities are set based on commonly observable factors such as student year of study or department.Mechanisms that utilize market equilibria fail to be strategy-proof when students can influence course prices. A mechanism is strategy-proof in the large if truthful reporting is approximately optimal in an environment with a large number of students. For market equilibria, this amounts to being strategy-proof in a limit market in which each student regards the market prices as exogenous to her reported preferences (Azevedo and Budish, 2019; Budish, 2011, see).77He et al. The French Revolution is what I described: a fundamental and brutal rewriting of the laws, institutions and principles that took a medieval country into the modern age. It is the foundational basis of our modern day societies (yes, partly including anglo ones, I'll come to that).

The false argument here is that this leftism is basically "destroying the elites in the name of lowering human quality down to the lowest of the low". This is why they insist so damn much on ultimately minor events of the Reign of Terror and ignore the long term virtuous aspects of it.

First off, this argument is false entirely: the French Revolution was a bourgeois revolution against an extremely privileged nobility that sought both liberty and equality.
"Privileged" in this case does not mean "rich". The French nobles were of an ancient, land-based wealth, which by the late 18th century was getting superseded by the nascent industries that the bourgeoisie owned. This is actually why the Revolution happened. Many merchants' revolts happened in French history (hell some did during the Hundred Years War), but by the 18th the merchants were financially stronger than the nobles.
"Privileges" at the time meant that the nobility was exempt from a tremendous amount of taxes and social charges that were left for the bourgeois and the peasantry to carry. "Ending the privileges" was the main cause for the Tennis Court Oath and the destruction of the Ancien Régime.

In this regard, the French Revolution must be understood as primarily a massive breakdown to kill the nobility-above-society system that had prevailed since the days of Charlemagne. Imbeciles and liars presume that this means "making nobleman equal to lowly peasants or bandits", absolutely no such thing was envisaged at all. You won't find a single document demanding that nobility or education or human qualities be degraded to a lower level, quite the contrary.

What it aimed for is a system that offered both liberty and equality. Equality meant equality before taxes and equal charges for all society before the State. Privileges were abolished, everyone paid taxes, everyone carried society together. Liberty meant that men were free to not be saddled with another man's undue privilege. For example the State was still 99% in the hands of the ancient nobility, with zero voting rights, zero functioning parliaments, zero chances to influence the national policies except by making a case in front of a privileged noble who was always going to say no to his privileges being infringed.

Thus the French Revolution ultimately produced what we'd call today a meritocratic system: whether noble or bourgeois (poor people were, in everyone's eyes, poor people), everyone had to compete for political power through the merits of their arguments (equality) and had no longer any right to impose their own weight on others and their property (liberty).

The liberty for the bourgeois who did the Revolution was first and foremost that of disposing of their own wealth. The equality was to not have a noble birth be a way to sit on their estates' wealth and demand that the rising bourgeois class pay for the extremely deep hole in French finances.

Checking the ethanol diversion policy and sugar stocks reaction.

India needs more sugar, so the government is taking sugar-based ethanol out of the 2026-27 equation.

Oil marketing companies issued a quantity-bid tender on 16 October for about 1,100 crore litres of ethanol for the supply year running November 2026 to October 2027. The tender states that the government has directed sugar diversion for ethanol to be reduced to zero. No offers have been sought for ethanol made from sugarcane juice, sugar, sugar syrup or B-heavy molasses.

Allowed feedstocks include maize, damaged food grains, surplus rice from FCI, C-heavy molasses and other materials permitted under the National Policy on Biofuels. The move follows concerns over domestic sugar availability and prices, with weaker rainfall in key cane states.

Sugar stocks reacted immediately. On 19 October, shares of Shree Renuka Sugars, Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar, Dwarikesh Sugar, Dhampur Sugar, Dalmia Bharat Sugar, Balrampur Chini, EID Parry and Triveni Engineering fell roughly 2–7% in early trade.

The policy logic is straightforward: less cane into ethanol, more cane into sugar. For mills that spent the last few years building ethanol capacity around juice, syrup and B-heavy molasses, the open question is what those plants earn when the higher-margin sugar-based routes are closed for this supply year. C-heavy molasses remains eligible, and grain-based routes are still open, but the flexibility mills had to switch between sugar and ethanol has narrowed.

The E20 blending target continues. The feedstock mix does not.

Abducted while hitchhiking in California in 1977, she was held captive and tortured for seven years after Hooker convinced her that a secret criminal organization would kill her family if she escaped.... 

In 1977, 20-year-old Colleen Stan was hitchhiking through California when a young couple stopped to offer her a ride. They had a baby in the car. They seemed harmless.

It would be seven years before she was free.

Cameron and Janice Hooker appeared to be an ordinary married couple. But shortly after picking Colleen up, Cameron threatened her with a knife and forced her into captivity.

For much of the next seven years, Colleen was kept inside a wooden box, often confined for up to 23 hours a day. She endured physical and psychological abuse while the couple continued their lives around her.

But Cameron’s most effective weapon wasn’t the box. It was a lie.

He convinced Colleen that a powerful underground organization called “The Company” was watching her every move. If she escaped or disobeyed, he claimed, its members would murder her family.

There was no such organization.

Yet the threat became so deeply embedded in Colleen’s mind that even when Cameron occasionally allowed her outside, she remained terrified of running away.

Incredibly, she was eventually permitted to visit her family. They noticed something was wrong, but Colleen was too frightened to reveal what was happening.

In 1984, Janice Hooker finally told Colleen that The Company did not exist. Colleen left Cameron, and Janice later reported his crimes to authorities.

Cameron was convicted in 1985 and sentenced to 104 years in prison.

Colleen survived an ordeal that remains one of America’s most disturbing documented cases of coercive control.

Her story revealed something profoundly unsettling about captivity: a prison doesn’t always need locked doors.

Sometimes, the captor makes the outside world seem even more dangerous than the cage.

text:
- Welcome to Keeneland: A Breeders' Cup Preview -
EP 0: 
A First-Timer's Guide/初めてレキシントンを訪れる方へ

Beyond the Breeders' Cup itself, Lexington, the Horse Capital of the World, and its surrounding countryside are well worth exploring for any racing fan fortunate enough to make the trip.
One memory that has stayed with me ever since my first visit is the view from the bus as it approached Lexington. The landscape suddenly opened up, revealing gently rolling green pastures stretching out on either side of the road, lined with seemingly endless white fences. In the evening sunlight, the silhouettes of grazing horses could be seen in the distance.
It's a sight that's difficult to forget.

- Getting to Lexington -
For international visitors, Kentucky isn't necessarily the most convenient destination to reach.
Lexington has its own airport, Blue Grass Airport (LEX), located just minutes from Keeneland. However, depending on where you're travelling from, it may be more practical to fly into a larger airport and complete the journey by road.
Nearby options include Cincinnati (approximately 1.5 hours by car), Indianapolis (around 3 hours), and Chicago (roughly 6 hours). Alternatively, connecting through major hubs such as New York or Atlanta to fly directly into Lexington is another possibility.

It's worth leaving some flexibility in your travel plans. Delays and cancellations are not uncommon in the US, and smaller airports tend to have fewer alternative services if something goes wrong.

Renting a car is highly recommended. Public transportation in this part of the country is limited(to say the least), and many of the places worth visiting are spread across the surrounding countryside. Without a car, getting around can be surprisingly painful😵‍💫.

- Places to Visit -
1. Keeneland Library
Located right on the Keeneland grounds, Keeneland Library is an absolute treasure for anyone interested in Thoroughbred history.
Established in 1939, it houses one of the world's largest collections of materials documenting the history and development of the Thoroughbred industry, including historical publications, photographs, racing records, pedigrees, and other invaluable resources.
The library is free to visit and normally opens to the public on weekdays, from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

2. Kentucky Horse Park
Of course, a visit to the Horse Capital of the World wouldn't be complete without spending some time with horses!
Kentucky Horse Park is an excellent place to start, particularly for visitors interested in different breeds and equestrian disciplines beyond Thoroughbred racing.
The park features breed demonstrations, equestrian exhibits, and the International Museum of the Horse. It is also home to the famous statue and final resting place of the legendary Man o' War.
General admission for adults is $28 during the 2026 main season.

3. Horse Farm Tours — VisitHorseCountry
One of the best opportunities Lexington offers is the chance to visit some of the world's most famous Thoroughbred farms.
Through Visit Horse Country, visitors can book guided tours of various farms and other equine facilities, with many tours costing approximately $20–40.
The choices are surprisingly diverse, ranging from major stallion operations such as Coolmore's Ashford Stud and Godolphin's Jonabell Farm to breeding farms and nurseries where young horses are raised. There are also opportunities to visit equine hospitals, feed production facilities, and other specialized parts of the industry.

Depending on the farm and the tour, visitors may have the chance to see foals, meet famous stallions or retired racehorses, and occasionally interact with the horses themselves.

For fellow Umamusume fans, some of these farms also have interesting historical connections. Symboli Kris S was born at Mill Ridge Farm, while Agnes Digital was bred at Runnymede Farm, both of which offer visitor tours.
Naturally, there may be little left to see directly connected to horses born decades ago, but visiting the places where their stories began can still make for a rather special kind of pilgrimage.

Farm tours become extremely popular around Breeders' Cup week, so booking early is strongly recommended.

Another important consideration is transportation. Many farms are located in relatively remote areas, and some do not allow visitors to arrive by taxi or rideshare. Always check the individual farm's requirements and arrange your return journey in advance.

For those without a car, organized horse-country tours listed on Tripadvisor or offered by local operators can be a good alternative, those typically include transportation throughout the visit.

4. Old Friends Thoroughbred Retirement Farm
If time allows, don't miss the chance to pay a visit to some old friends.

Located in nearby Georgetown, Old Friends is one of the world's best-known Thoroughbred retirement farms, providing a home for hundreds of retired racehorses over the years.

Among the horses laid to rest here are Charismatic(sire of Wonder Acute) and War Emblem, both of whom spent time in Japan, while its current residents include familiar names such as Silver Charm(he also went to Asia for stud), I'll Have Another(he also stood in Japan at Big Red Farm), and Big Brown.

For a modest admission fee, visitors can join a guided tour, meet some of the retired horses up close, offer treats where permitted, and hear the remarkable stories behind their racing careers and lives after retirement.

The general tour costs $30 and lasts approximately 90 minutes.
For anyone who has followed these horses over the years, meeting them in retirement can be a particularly memorable experience.

5. Keeneland November Breeding Stock Sale
The Keeneland November Breeding Stock Sale begins on November 3, just a few days after the championships.
As one of the world's most important Thoroughbred breeding stock auctions, it offers a look into another side of the racing industry. Some horses that have recently competed at the highest level, potentially including Breeders' Cup participants, may also appear in the sales.
Visitors interested in bloodstock and breeding can observe the public auction, provided they respect the normal operations of the sale and avoid disturbing horses, handlers, or buyers.

6. A Little Further Away: Louisville
For those with extra time, Louisville is another destination worth considering.

Home to Churchill Downs and the Kentucky Derby Museum, the city offers an opportunity to explore the history of America's most famous horse race.

Morning workout experiences are also available at both Churchill Downs and Keeneland, with guided tours offered at selected times. Be sure to check the relevant schedules and ticket requirements in advance.

For Breeders' Cup week in 2026, Keeneland is also hosting free morning workout viewing from October 26–29, with additional paid tour options.

- Watching the Breeders' Cup at Keeneland -
Compared with a vast racecourse like Tokyo Racecourse, Keeneland is relatively compact, particularly around its grandstand and spectator facilities.

But that is also part of its charm.
The grounds are exceptionally beautiful, with a distinctive atmosphere that feels quite different from the enormous metropolitan racecourses familiar to many international fans. Depending on the viewing area, spectators can get remarkably close to the track and the horses.

During the Breeders' Cup, official merchandise shops will be set up around the venue, along with race-day publications and other souvenirs worth looking out for.

One practical warning, however: parking and getting in and out of Keeneland during major race meetings can be rather chaotic.

With the enormous crowds expected for the Breeders' Cup, it's important to check the official parking and shuttle arrangements beforehand, and to allow plenty of time for departure after racing.

On-site parking is limited, and official park-and-ride services are available. Race-day admission tickets should also be purchased in advance.
---

Wishing everyone a wonderful Breeders' Cup, and welcome to Keeneland!

text:
What Witkoff brought to Putin

Trump's special envoy didn't arrive light. The entire European world had assembled a folder for him: Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Støre, Finnish President Stubb, and emissaries from France, Britain, Germany, Poland, the EU, and NATO. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined via video.

The participants themselves published the luggage inventory. It contained a document outlining possible security guarantees for Ukraine, including something similar to Article 5 of the NATO Charter, which stipulates that all rise in defense of one. A partial ceasefire on energy and food infrastructure, plus a moratorium on fighting in the Black Sea—to restore grain supplies. A "prosperity plan" for post-war Ukraine, a new "European security architecture." And the cherry on top: a trilateral summit between Putin, Trump, and Zelenskyy. The latter clarified that only the leaders would discuss the territories.

If you peel back the diplomatic veneer, Kyiv is asking for silence in the skies above its thermal power plants and in the seas around its ports. Zelenskyy has offered this bluntly: Ukraine won't attack Russian refineries, and Russia won't attack Ukrainian energy. A ceasefire is in place where it hurts.
Not a word about the land.

What's the mood of the courier delivering the package? In recent weeks, Trump has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel. Negotiations with the Ukrainians at the Whitkoff Golf Club near Miami were prematurely concluded because of this news. Trump himself argued that it was time for Ukraine to change its president, or at least its negotiator, and Vice President Vance called it "a partner of sorts." Not an ally. Meanwhile, Kyiv was experiencing ballistic missile launch data loss, Starlink speeds were dropping, and Patriot missiles were delayed.

So, in Oslo, Zelenskyy was largely buying back what had been disconnected. He thanked him for the missile warnings "now working" and received a promise to restore Starlink within 48 hours. And then he blurted out, "We're not losing the war, but we're losing people." A few hours later, Trump again doubted he even wanted peace. He promised that without a deal, things would be "very bad."

Sergey Lavrov voiced our position the day before: "We'll see what they offer. If they offer something that benefits us economically and financially, then why not? But this must be done without any political concessions on our part."

The humanitarian part will be the easiest to handle. Trump personally requested the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 72-year-old American sentenced to six years and ten months for fighting for the Ukrainian Armed Forces as a mercenary. According to ABC, several prisoners are involved.

The economics will be heard. The Kremlin is only allowing a meeting with Zelenskyy in Moscow, and, according to Peskov, it is "impossible" at the G20 summit in Miami.

We already had an energy truce in the spring of 2025, and granting a second respite while the enemy's power generation is crumbling is strangely generous. For Ukraine, "Article 5" is a NATO fence along our borders, where it all began. No Western troop presence in our independent country. And without it, Article 5 is toothless.

While diplomats haggle over the sky and sea, the fate of the land is decided by the front. And every subsequent proposal will arrive on Bankova Street with a smaller map of Ukraine...
